title: Looking for Neem Karoli Baba: How a 20th century guru found a new generation
content:
A little before 6 pm, hundreds wait in the slow drizzle for the aarti to begin. Somewhere in the middle, a woman stands with her palms folded in prayer, her tear-streaked face lit up by the aarti fire. Just then, the bells toll, and she joins the crowd to chant a guttural “Sitaram, Sitaram”.
One of the most influential Indian spiritual gurus of the 20th century, the height of Neem Karoli Baba’s fame coincided with the Western spiritual counterculture movement of the 1960s and 1970s. Like his contemporary Mahesh Yogi, whose ashram in Rishikesh famously hosted the Beatles in 1968, Neem Karoli Baba’s influence spread globally through his prominent American disciples. Among them, Richard Alpert, the Harvard psychologist who became Ram Dass and whose Be Here Now is considered a landmark text for spiritual seekers, American rock singer-turned-kirtan singer Krishna Das (born Jeffrey Kagel), and Dr Larry Brilliant, the American epidemiologist who is globally renowned for his role in eradicating smallpox.
But modern interest around the Baba was piqued possibly around 2015, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited the Facebook headquarters in California, where Mark Zuckerberg spoke about a “difficult period” in his life when Apple founder Steve Jobs is said to have advised him to visit the Kainchi Dham shrine in India that Jobs had himself visited.
Since then, in a country that’s in a constant search for cultural anchors, the crowds haven’t stopped coming to Kainchi Dham.
According to the district administration, 24.34 lakh people visited Kainchi Dham in the first six months of 2026, compared with around eight lakh visitors a year in the previous years.
But it’s one visit that everyone in Kainchi Dham and the surrounding Kainchi village talks about. In 2022, power couple Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma, along with their daughter, visited the Baba’s ashrams in Kainchi Dham and Vrindavan.
Modern interest around the Baba was piqued around 2015.
“The Kainchi we grew up in was a lot quieter, but after Virat Kohli and Anushka visited the shrine, the crowds wouldn’t stop coming. Since I was a child, June 15, the day Maharaj ji established the ashram here, has been celebrated as a festival. But now, Kainchi looks like there is a festival everyday,” Dheeraj Tiwari, 27, says.
He isn’t complaining, though. Tiwari runs a shop beside the Kainchi Dham ashram, where he sells boxes of peda and “Baba Kambal”, the kind of plaid woollen blankets that Neem Karoli Baba is seen wearing in all his photographs. Similar checked blankets are given as offerings at the shrine, with devotees referring to the Baba’s iconic blanket-wrapped reclining pose as the “Kambal Mudra” and associating it with Lord Hanuman’s posture when he blocked Bhima’s path. Some of his followers even consider him a reincarnation of Lord Hanuman.
“Only Raymond blankets are given to the Baba as offering,” says Tiwari, going on to talk about his tryst with the Baba’s “chamatkaar”.
A few years ago, he says, when he decided to set up his blanket shop, he needed a distributor for Raymond blankets. “I had no idea where to find one. But then, that very day, a Raymond agent arrived in Kainchi. My family has been running a restaurant here since the 1990s, now we run this business, too. Sab Babaji ki kripa…my life is a gift that Baba ji has given me,” he says, folding his hands and slipping into a few moments of reverence.
Much of what is known about the Baba is through devotional biographies, accounts of those who lived around the same time as him, and now, the movie. According to these accounts, the Baba was born around 1900 into a wealthy Brahmin family in Akbarpur, in Uttar Pradesh’s Firozabad district, as Lakshman Narayan Sharma. Married as a child, he is said to have left home at 12, with the subsequent years marked by long periods of wandering across Rajasthan, Gujarat and later, Uttar Pradesh. There are accounts of how he went back to his village at one point, only to wander again. In Uttar Pradesh, he travelled to Neeb Karori village in Farrukhabad district and meditated here, an association that stayed in his name.
Neem Karoli Baba’s first temple, Hanuman Garhi (Express)
By the early 1950s, the wandering ascetic had begun creating places of worship. His first temple was Hanuman Garhi, built on the Manora hillside in Nainital. Over the next two decades, temples and in some places ashrams followed — at Bhumiyadhar, Kainchi and Kakrighat in Uttarakhand, Vrindavan, Kanpur and Lucknow in UP, and Shimla and Delhi, among other places.
Kainchi Dham, whose Hanuman temple was consecrated on June 15, 1964, eventually became the principal ashram of his later years.
⠀
A little after 6 pm, the crowd moves towards the Kainchi shrine barefoot. Devotees leave their footwear outside and step onto the cold stone floor, moving through steel railings and barricades that guide them towards the sanctum. There are no separate queues for VIPs. A little ahead is a white marble statue of the Baba, complete with the blanket in marble.
The Shipra River runs by the ashram, the sound of its rushing waters a constant soundtrack that’s audible above the bells and the bhajan of devotees.
This weekend, the packed road outside the shrine, wet after a sudden shower, glistens with lights from the shops on either side. Kainchi’s local economy runs entirely on Baba’s name — “his blessings”, is how the traders say that — with shops selling his photographs, trinkets, blankets and prasad.
Metres away, Vishesh Kaushik, 26, an IIT Kanpur graduate from Gurgaon, waits outside Hotel Monal for his room to be handed over. He says he decided to come to Kainchi after watching Hanuman Ansh. “I am usually not impulsive,” he says. “But after watching the movie, I opened the RedBus app, booked a ticket and came here.”
Neem Karoli Baba’s fame coincided with the Western spiritual counterculture movement of the 1960s and 1970s.
Kaushik, who recently lost two members of his family, says the film affected him more deeply than he expected. “I cried several times while watching it,” he says. “But here, I feel a sense of peace.”
Talking of the film, he says he was particularly struck by a scene in which Baba is shown eating seeds and producing plants from his mouth.
To Kaushik, the moment represented something larger than a cinematic miracle. “That is the power to create life,” he says.
At 7 pm, the temple closes. Red curtains are drawn across the rooms where the deities sit, and the gates are shut. Devotees who have failed to make it inside stand outside, pleading with the authorities to let them in. Some cry, others wait in the hope that the doors might reopen.
Then, Kainchi changes almost immediately. The shops begin to close and the crowd thins out.
Vineeta Rawat, 27, who grew up in Bhowali, a town 10 km from Kainchi village, and who now works at Hotel Monal, says, “Once the mandir shuts down, it feels like Kainchi has gone to bed.”
⠀
On a Friday night in state capital Dehradun, the 8 pm show of Hanuman Ansh at the city’s Pacific Mall is packed. Families with children and the elderly, and young people in groups, all watching the story of a guru.
As the young Shobhinaw Satya, who plays the Baba, appears on screen, there’s none of the hooting and whistling that usually accompany the hero’s entry; only a reverential silence.
One of the scenes has a group of children teasing the Baba as he meditates in a lake. He then miraculously pulls out laddoos from the water and gives it to each of the children. In the movie hall, a young girl turns to her sister and asks, “Aise sach mein hota hai kya? (Does this really happen?)”
Later, as a man lost in the forests around Kainchi begins reciting the Hanuman Chalisa, the audience joins in.
When the lights come on, people linger to take photographs, some make reels with photos of the Baba that appear on the screen along with the rolling credits, and others continue sitting, wiping their eyes.
Anupriya Nagar, 21, one of the three producers of the film, says she was doing her Bachelor’s in Economics at the University of Bath, UK, when she came across the story of how Steve Jobs met Neem Karoli.
The daughter of an art collector, Nagar had already secured a job at an art company in Zurich and had hoped to graduate and leave for Switzerland. Instead, she found herself drawn to the story of the Indian spiritual guru.
Back in India, Ragini Sona, a family friend, introduced her to the team making Hanuman Ansh. Nagar, who read 120 pages of the script, recalls “getting goosebumps”. She offered to pitch in with the production, along with Sona and Namrata Singh, leading to an all-woman team of producers. “The movie should have been made long ago. I believe spirituality is in every one of us; we need to find a way to access it.”
⠀
Over 400 km from the Kainchi Ashram is Akbarpur, a village in Firozabad district that’s the birthplace of the Baba.
Though the village has a temple that came up in 2001, where his stone statue shares space with those of Lord Hanuman, Lord Vishnu and Goddess Lakshmi, Akbarpur isn’t awash in the kind of devotion that keeps Kainchi going. When they talk of him here, it is as “Lakshman Das ji”, a mortal among mortals, the father of two sons and a daughter, a man who left his family behind and found fame elsewhere.
It doesn’t help that a property tussle has been playing out in Akbarpur between the Baba’s granddaughters and a Trust, which manages the temple and the family property. Six daughters of the Baba’s younger son, Dharam Narayan Sharma, have written to the District Magistrate seeking action against the illegal occupation of their ancestral house in Akbarpur.
Shyam Upadhyay, a farmer, says that as long as Lakshman Das walked through these lanes, he was not “Baba”, just an ordinary householder with a family.
In her brick house behind the temple, Shanti Jatav, who says she is around 85 years old, claims to have met Lakshman Das ji. “On the day Lakshman Das set out on his journey, his wife Rambeti did not even weep,” she says.
But now, Akbarpur is hoping the Baba’s popularity will help the villagers’ cause.
There’s a quiet excitement about a new ring road or a parikrama path that’s being built around the village. People also hope that the other roads in the village will finally be fixed, and that dirty water won’t pool in the lanes anymore.
On a platform just outside the family’s dak bungalow are two pairs of charan paduka (footprint-shaped markers) commemorating the Baba’s two sons, Aneg Singh Sharma and Dharam Narayan Sharma, who died during the Covid wave. People come, quietly bow their heads, and leave.
A prayer niche in a Jatav household in Akbarpur, where Ambedkar and Neem Karauli Baba now share a wall. (Express Photo by Deepak Tenguriya)
The government has now announced that the region will be part of a larger tourist circuit. The village hopes all of this will add up to something.
A labourer on the outskirts of the village says, “The cremation ground is without a roof and it’s difficult to cremate bodies in the rain. Maybe now, they’ll build a roof?”
As the day winds down, we find ourselves at a doorway. Inside, a framed photograph of Ambedkar hangs tilted on the exposed brick wall. On a shelf below it are framed pictures of Gods, and one of the Baba. The young man who lives here sees no contradiction in an iconoclast sharing space with Gods and godmen. “We believe in all. Whatever we are today, we owe to Ambedkar ji, but Neem Karoli Baba is our village’s pride, so we worship him too.”

title: ‘Echoes of the Past’: Repatriations of three Fort Peck children bring joy, tears
content:
WARNING: This story has photos of caskets and contains disturbing details about residential and boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here are healing-informed resources from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition in the U.S. The National Indian Residential School Crisis Hotline in Canada can be reached at 1-866-925-4419 or the Lamathut Crisis Line at 1-800-721-0066. If you’re in Treaty 4 territory, call 306-522-7494.
Charles Fox
Special to ICT
FORT PECK, Montana — The last handful of soil drifted through the air and down upon the casket, marking an historic moment in the decades-long quest by the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes to bring home their children.
More than 135 years after leaving home for the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, Christine Redstone, Peter Howe and Richard Morgan have been reburied under the big sky of Montana, with the whispers of a breeze coming off the Missouri River.
They finally are resting in the earth that contains the echoes of their past.
The three children were part of a group of 43 students who arrived after an 1800-mile journey from Fort Peck to the Pennsylvania school, arriving on April 15,1890. The school, the first federally run off-reservation boarding school, was known for its “kill the Indian, save the man” motto initiated by founder Richard Pratt to suppress Native culture and languages. Nearly 8,000 students attended during its 39 years of existence, and many, like Christine, Peter and Richard, never made it home.
Finally, this year, the three children were repatriated back to their homeland, bringing a lasting impact to their community.
Organizers had stressed in the weeks and months leading up to the homecoming of “the community becoming the family,” and the need to make sure “no child comes home alone.” Family members greeted Christine’s remains, but Richard and Peter do not have living relatives.
The messages translated into reality over three days, producing large processions and caravans, nightly community meals, and children dancing in the headlights of parked cars while preparations were made for all-night vigils.
“It’s been a wonderful time to see the families gather, to give love to one another, for us to laugh, for us to cry, for us to hold close to each other, and for our young people to learn how we’re all related and how all those connections connect to one another…not let it just be a temporary thing, but to strengthen those family ties for future generations,” Jonny BearCub said in her prayer at the service for Christine Thursday, Sept. 10, at the Freda Fourstar Community Hall.
“They (the children) are coming home at an opportune time to remind us that we’re only as strong as our families are strong. We’re only as strong as our tribe is strong. A nation is only as strong as its people,” BearCub continued in her prayer.
‘How fleeting freedom really is’
The level of participation and enthusiasm was especially evident by the procession leading up to the reburial of Howe and Morgan in the tribal repatriation cemetery. Students from Poplar High School ran the distance, while equestrians and a caravan of cars followed closely behind. They were led by an orange fire engine affectionately known as the “Big Orange Pumpkin.”
But the celebratory spirit did not mask the obstacles they overcame to bring the children home.
Well over a decade ago, Darrell “Curley” Youpee, who died in May 2021, and Ken Ryan had tried to initiate bringing Christine home at the family’s request.
For Richard and Peter, the difficulties were greater since they did not have living relatives, a requirement from the Office of Army Cemeteries that has been challenged by tribes in court.
Finally, the Office of Army Cemeteries agreed to let a tribal representative sign on behalf of enrolled members, and Dyan Youpee, the tribe’s cultural preservation director, was able to bring her late father’s efforts to fruition.
“He set the bar really high to be an anthropologist, an archeologist, historian, museum curator, and an archivist. … I learned to fight harder,” Youpee said.
“For people who never experienced repatriation, there’s the fighting with the agencies to bring [the children] back, the organizing, the planning, and the difficulties of getting different families together,” Youpee told the crowd at Christine’s pre-burial service. “I really fought a lot of battles, and I didn’t win all of them.”
But there was also sadness that many who worked hard for the day and dreamed of seeing the children returned home had passed away.
“I know that Ken [Ryan], my dad, and Lana Fourstar’s grandma and mom, they really wanted to be here and be a part of it,” Youpee said. “There were a lot of people in the community who wanted to witness this, and they’re not here.”
While the celebratory spirit and the return of the remains of the three children could bring some healing to families and the tribe, it would never produce closure to a period of Native American history that affected most every Native family and produced generational scars.
“We cannot comprehend the grief that our families went through long ago,” BearCub said as she led those assembled in prayer. “We can only be angry for them. But help us to understand that our rage and our anger that our ancestors felt, and use that as a power to fuel ourselves to be better than those who took our children. Help us to use that rage and anger to make us stronger, to make us more compassionate, to make us be able to understand people who are different from ourselves.”
She continued, “For with the return of our children, we understand how fleeting freedom really is. For in those days, the government came and took them.”
A message to future generations
Peter and Richard are now buried in the tribal repatriation cemetery in Poplar, while Christine lies to the west in the Oswego Catholic Cemetery, where she is reunited with other family members. Both locations are dramatically different from the cemetery at the Carlisle Barracks, where the act of stripping away individuality and culture were taken to a new level after death.
The students who were not lucky enough to survive Carlisle found themselves represented by identical, white gravestones lined up in straight lines like a formation of soldiers.
At Christine’s wake, Dylan Youpee, one of the spiritual leaders on the journey, described the cemetery and the emotions stirred by the visit.
“You think it’s just a cemetery, something that you see all the time on the side of the road,” Dylan Youpee said. “But when you go around that corner and you see those headstones of all those Indian kids, holy smokes. That lump comes up in your throat and your first reaction is to be sad, is to cry. And then you get another emotion. You get angry. You want to get angry because these people took our kids. These people took our children, brought them all the way over here, 1,800 miles over here, and beat the Indian out of them…Pretty soon you want to leave because of it. You want to leave that place. But then a part of you wants to stay… You want to make sure the relatives are brought back.”
At events over a three-day repatriation period in Montana, various relatives, spiritual and tribal leaders spoke about the experience of visiting the grounds of the former boarding school and the repatriation process. The emotional duress of walking in the footsteps of ancestors, especially those who never made it back home, dominated their talks.
But out of the somber darkness and raw emotions there was the light of inspiration created by the students who endured the experience.
“There were some difficult things that our ancestors went through like those young children dying, separated from their families,” said Barry Bighorn, a member of the Fort Peck Tribal Executive Board. “But for the majority of them, they didn’t lose what was inside of them, how they were raised, and they stayed strong. They learned. They succeeded. And that’s what stuck with me, is how, how well they did, how they overcame those difficult circumstances.”
Bighorn said there are lessons for the current generations.
“It’s a reminder to us today,” he said. “It brings that message home to us to love your families, love your children…. A lot of those children [in Carlisle] didn’t get to have that their whole life here. And a lot of the parents didn’t get to have time with their children because they were taken from them … It’s a different world that we live in now. There’s no reason for our children to go away like that anymore. So, consider that a blessing…We’re still here. We still have our identities and our families.”
‘She wanted to come home’
Throughout the homecoming, an inspiring image of Christine began to emerge, though little is known about Peter and not even a photograph can be found of Richard, who died of tuberculosis less than a year after arriving at Carlisle.
“Today, you look around what this young lady [Christine] brought us, it helps us understand the importance of compassion, empathy, caring, sharing, loving, our patience, our generosity,” said Michael Turcotte, who served as master of ceremonies for the reburials. “All these things she’s instilled in us, in our development of our own self.”
The five female relatives of Christine who traveled to Carlisle spoke about how they had gained a clearer image of who Christine was.
Michael Redstone describes how years ago, early in the process, she would imagine Christine.
“I would shut my eyes and I could see the prairie, and I could see that she wanted to come back, and she didn’t want to stay there,” she said. “I had to go back and get her. But, I didn’t know how.”
She learned along the way, with the help of Dyan Youpee. She also learned more about Christine, who spent nine years at Carlisle.
“When I got to Carlisle, I got to learn more about her,” Michael Redstone said. “She became more human to me, and not some ancestor that I’ve never known, but my actual grandma. I got to know her and know that she’s like us. She was a hard worker. She liked to play the mandolin and I’m pretty sure she had a wicked sense of humor… One of my cousins told me that she had a dream about Christine and that all she wanted was to be with her family and to hear a good song.”
But the emotions of Carlisle took their toll.
“I remember calling home three days in, and saying, ‘I’m done. I’m ready. I want to come home,’” Michael Redstone said. “I could just imagine what she had to deal with, being there for so long. But I like to think … the other Fort Peck kids all helped each other and all kept each other going and kept supporting each other.”
She, too, felt the impact of stepping into the cemetery.
“I started to get emotional the minute I walked into the cemetery, and then when I saw where she was buried for myself for the first time… it just hit me, and then it made me cry, and I dropped to my knees, and I just sobbed because it was so overwhelming,” she said.
“After so long, I was finally able to see her there. Like she was there in person.”
Now that the journey has reached its end, there is time for Michael Redstone to reflect and to heal with the hope that one day there will no longer be children in a cemetery in Carlisle.
“It does give me some peace because I feel like there’s a part of me that was missing, and it makes me feel more whole knowing that a member of my family got to come home and gets to rest with our relatives,” Michael Redstone said.
“It gives me some peace to know that she’s home and that she no longer has to be by herself where nobody can visit her and properly mourn her,” she continued. “What a privilege it is to be at the end of your life, to be buried next to your loved ones. There are kids over there that are still waiting. I keep hoping and praying that eventually, that cemetery’s going to be empty. That there’s nobody left there. Everybody’s going to get to go home, and everybody’s going to get to be with their families.”

title: Lack of volunteers sees Pride events cancelled in regional WA
content:
Low volunteer numbers see pride events cancelled in regional WA, but there is one bright spot
Organisers of queer festivals in regional Western Australia say their events are at risk of vanishing due to a lack of people willing to help coordinate every year, as another Pride parade bites the dust.
In Carnarvon, about 900 kilometres north of Perth, those pressures have brought the town's 2026 parade to an end after three years, despite being well supported in the community.
Most of the committee behind Queernarvon has stepped down or moved away, leaving the group without enough volunteers.
In the state's south, Busselton's long-running Pride parade has also been cancelled, with organisers instead directing their limited resources towards education and wellbeing events.
But in the Pilbara, a Pride festival that began as a small games night among friends has grown to attract about 1,500 people, with organisers crediting support from the wider community for its success.
So, what are the obstacles for LGTBIQA+ people living in the regions?
Changing views
Queernarvon chair Carmen Reilly said Pride events played an important role in regional communities.
In her view, there had been a shift in public perception towards trans, gender diverse and young LGBTQI+ people.
"I have had several conversations over the last few months with people who have never met a trans person, but have seen posts and AI clips on social media and have formed their opinions," she said.
"I say to those people, 'If you're basing your opinions and ideas on social media, put the phone down, go out and meet someone who has a different life experience to you.'"
She said events such as these helped build real connections within communities.
"There's more connecting us than dividing us,"she said.
Finding a community
Johnathan Trace, who is working in Carnarvon on a holiday visa, said he made the decision to leave his home country of the United States because the rise of the far right made him feel unsafe as a trans man.
"I was like, 'It's time. I need to get out of here,'" he said.
Since being in Australia, Mr Trace said he had felt safer but still experienced moments that made him feel unsafe and unwelcome.
Those ranged from nasty comments delivered by strangers in the bathroom, to homophobic outbursts from customers he was serving at work.
Mr Trace said it was a shame the Carnarvon event was cancelled, as there were a lack of spaces to discuss his life experiences as a trans man.
"You're surrounded by all these backpackers who are just here for a good time, who don't want to talk about politics or anything that ruins their good vibes," Mr Trace said.
"It's very hard to find a real community where you can talk about your queerness and the negative things you face with that."
Mining towns lead the way
A bright spot for WA Pride celebrations is in the state's mining region.
The Pilbara Pride Festival started from a small games night among friends, but is now in its fifth year, with about 1,500 people estimated to attend the events across places such as Port Hedland, Karratha and Onslow.
Port Hedland Lesbian, Allies, Gays Society (PHLAGS+) secretary Gloria Jacob put the success down to dedicated volunteers and support from local government and the resources sector.
"This year in particular, the one thing that filled my cup was the high school students asking us to hold a workshop at the school, and the high school allowing us to do that," Ms Jacob said.
But she said it had not always been this way.
"I can tell you there were times in the early days where it wasn't that pleasant, and it still isn't pleasant," she said.
"But the main reason we do it is to ensure our young people, our First Nations people and those who are less able to access these safe spaces know PHLAGS+ exist."
'Space to be themselves'
A local church initially protested against the PHLAGS+ Pride events.
"But the second year they actually marched with us in the parade," Ms Jacob said.
"The more people engage and the more people become aware — it becomes the norm."
Ms Jacob said if support was not upheld by the wider community, the regions will lose their diversity.
"If they don't feel like they are welcome or supported or have space to be themselves openly, you're going to lose them to the city,"she said.
"The city can be brought to the communities, we've proven it through Pilbara Pride."

title: Can Community Programs Reduce Gun Violence?
content: A new study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years. This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years. According to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship. We found that the Fellowship contributed to long-term reductions in violence, and that the declines only grew as the program operated.” Other UC Berkeley coauthors include Jason Corburn; Mahasin Mujahid, chair of the Division of Epidemiology; Sean Darling-Hammond; and Juan Cabrera. Sam Vaughn, director of ONS, said, “The statistics back up what we have seen in the streets: fewer shootings, fewer deaths, and a healthier community overall.” Homicide rates are down across the country; the FBI recently released data showing murder rates are down a record 18.1% nationally. However, Richmond has consistently outperformed national declines for over a decade, suggesting the results are due to that city’s innovative, street-outreach interventions and their mentorship of active firearm offenders, a program called Operation Peacemaker Fellowship, which was instituted in 2010. The Fellowship uses a public health approach to preventing gun violence. According to James Houston, the program manager of the ONS who oversees the day-to-day implementation of the Peacemaker Fellowship, including managing 14 street-outreach workers who currently serve 123 participants, “the credit goes to the young people making better decisions and the team that gives them support, mentorship, and encouragement every day to make a change.” According to Shasa Curl, Richmond city manager, Richmond had over 300 police officer full-time equivalent in 2014 and 180 in 2020, but was down to 121 active sworn officers by 2024. Yet during this time, the ONS, through continued city support and grants, was able to expand its staff and increase the number of fellows and participants. Even during the COVID-19 period, the study shows Richmond did not have as significant a spike in firearm violence as most cities did across the Bay Area and nationally. According to the ONS, the health impacts are lives saved, safer streets, and community members with a renewed positive life outlook. One former Peacemaker Fellowship participant said, “Before the ONS came to me, I didn’t care if I survived past 19, as long as I had a name in the streets. After my experience with the ONS, with my mentor coming at me every day, I got support for my stress, got a job, paying my bills, and have a kid now. I’m no longer terrorizing my community.” The paper notes the cascading health benefits for entire communities when gun violence reductions are sustained, such as the case in Richmond. Further research will explore how unique aspects of the ONS might be contributing to declines in gun violence, including that the program is a city government agency, independent from the police department, has had consistent funding, has trained and retained many of the same outreach workers for over a decade (these city staff are well paid with benefits), and delivers individualized supports to each participant based on their needs, such as food and housing assistance, cognitive behavioral therapy, addiction and anger management counseling, and other social services aimed at both reducing gun violence risk and addressing trauma. This article was originally published on Berkeley Public Health News. Read the original article.

title: Wildfire strategy doesn't need a winner—with 3 camps fighting for dominance, the system can't keep up with the risk
content:
One of the problems with how America deals with wildfires is the belief that there is one primary strategy that can end the nation's wildfire crisis. Whether that's detecting and putting out every fire fast, increasing logging and forest thinning, or allowing fires to burn under safe conditions, the default choice today is to pour more money and effort into the star approach of the moment.
But an effective wildfire strategy in the face of worsening fire seasons demands a system of actions—interconnected pieces that reinforce one another.
Right now, those pieces mostly are not connected. Research groups, governments and organizations tend to separate into distinct camps, each promoting its own specific strategy. The result is a system that can't keep up with the rising fire risk.
Our team of researchers, along with fire ecologist Jim Menakis, who recently retired from the U.S. Forest Service, has been looking at wildfires from social, ecological and risk-science perspectives to help forest and fire managers and communities in fire-prone areas turn research into practices that can reduce fire-related risks.
We have seen the pitfalls of current fire management approaches and also examples of what actually works.
Three separate camps
Wildfire strategy tends to break into three distinct camps today, each focusing heavily on one approach over the others.
One camp wants to double down on suppressing every ignition quickly and aggressively, contending that it's the surest way to prevent immediate loss. The direction to put out every fire quickly has been a foundation of the U.S. government response to wildfires since the early 1900s and persists despite attempts over the years to change it.
A second camp says the real problem is fuel: flammable vegetation that has been piling up for decades in forests and rangelands because of too much fire suppression.
This group's solution is to scale up forest and brush thinning through logging and controlled burning. Calls for these actions span political administrations, from the U.S. Forest Service's Wildfire Crisis Strategy during the Biden administration to the Trump administration's 2025 executive order calling for the expansion of American timber production and rescinding protections for roadless areas of national forests. But while excessive fuel is a problem, particularly during dry periods, it isn't the only issue.
A third camp says fire is coming regardless, and people have to live with it by accepting and promoting more fire, but allowing it to burn on our terms, when and where it's safe. This is often called managed wildfire. It sometimes includes creating landscapes and communities that can survive and recover from fire.
Each camp tends to operate in isolation from the others, often with its own budget, workforce, practices and culture. These silos can inhibit communication and coordination, which can make fire management less effective.
Success stories at the intersections
The question for fire management shouldn't be "which of the three is right?" It should be "where do they reinforce each other?"
Successful fire strategies combine many approaches to lower risk. If you look closely, you can see some of the ways these methods intersect.
Fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning of vegetation and forest thinning, used in the right locations, don't stop fires on their own, but they can make suppression safer and more effective by lowering a fire's intensity.
Using prescribed burns and forest thinning strategically can also make it safer for managers to allow lower-intensity fire to expand under favorable weather conditions, thereby dampening future fire risk and letting fire play its ecological role in renewing natural systems. A fire meant to spread still needs a safe edge to stop at, and fuel treatments serve this purpose.
And while suppression and the idea of living with fire appear to oppose each other, the same detection and real-time decision tools that let crews hit a fire hard and fast are exactly the tools needed to allow a fire to burn under safe conditions. Living with fire becomes credible only after fuel treatments have lowered risk to communities.
A place where everyone is working together
Wildfire activity has increased markedly across many parts of the U.S. in recent decades, resulting in destruction in communities, harm to water supplies and tragic fatalities. We believe that changing this trajectory requires a shift in thinking, from promoting a single "best" wildfire strategy to designing stronger connections between strategic options.
Building these connections has to begin long before a fire starts, continue while the fire burns and endure long after the fire has ended. It includes how fire research and fire-risk-reduction projects are designed and funded, how communities are brought into planning to build trust and support, and how communities can lessen their vulnerability to wildfires, such as home hardening, developing escape routes and updating land-use codes.
Reducing fire risk isn't solely the responsibility of a single government agency or private entity; all sectors of society must contribute.
This is already happening where people are willing to do the hard work.
For example, the Northern Colorado Fireshed Collaborative brings together federal and state agencies, local governments, water utilities and residents. It coordinates reducing flammable vegetation across land ownership boundaries, prepares homeowners and communities through education and financial assistance for wildfire prevention measures, and organizes response and recovery efforts as one connected system rather than separate ones.
Everyone has a role
The wildfire problem exceeds what any single entity can effectively tackle on its own.
Fire scientists, government agencies and local communities all play a role, which means you do, too. Check whether your area has a fire collaborative or community wildfire protection plan. Show up to public meetings to stay informed, and start making an impact at home by clearing dry brush around your property and helping neighbors do the same.
The path to better strategies is built by people working together, not by policy on a page.

title: From Durham to Zimbabwe: Young Constitution Defenders keep the democratic flame burning
content:
By Correspondent
THERE was something deeply symbolic about a group of young Zimbabweans gathering in Durham, in the North East of England, to discuss the future of a country more than 11 hours away from home. They were far from Zimbabwe geographically, but their conversation demonstrated that distance does not necessarily weaken a person’s connection to home.
Instead, for the young people associated with the Constitution Defenders Forum of Zimbabwe (CDF), being abroad has become another platform from which they can speak about the Constitution, democratic accountability and the future of their country.
The Durham meeting coincided with the birthday of Patson Muzuwa, turning what might otherwise have been an ordinary birthday occasion into a gathering of friendship, patriotism and political reflection. Which looked like a handover of the button from old class to youth by Muzuwa.
The atmosphere was one of hope rather than despair. The young people spoke about Zimbabwe with the familiarity of people who may be living thousands of miles away but who still carry their country in their hearts. Their message was clear: leaving Zimbabwe does not mean abandoning Zimbabwe. Indeed, for some members of the diaspora, the distance has made their concern about the country’s constitutional direction even more pronounced.
The Durham gathering brought together young Zimbabweans who demonstrated that political consciousness is not restricted by geography. There was celebration, friendship and fellowship, but there was also serious discussion about the Constitution and the country’s political future. The meeting provided an opportunity for the youths to reflect on the importance of constitutional safeguards at a time when Zimbabwe has undergone another major constitutional controversy.
The young people did not gather simply to complain about their country. They gathered because they believe Zimbabwe can be better. Their hope is that constitutionalism can ultimately prevail and that the country’s institutions can be strengthened in a manner that protects citizens rather than political office holders. This is what made the gathering significant. The youths were not in Harare. They were not sitting in Parliament. Names included Anna Katsande, Felistas W Munemo, Samuel Jambaya, Ettar Patience Mhlanga, Happiness Ncube, Fadzai Mavenganise, Prince Justin Chihurani, Felicia W Munemo, Michelle Rwatiringa, Tsitsidzashe Truth Parere, Sindiso Ndlovu, Tatenda Muza, Brian Murenza, Andrew Tinashe Masuka, Tanyaradzwa Emily Daka, Tatenda Nyikayaramba and a group of elders that supported the Durham gathering of John Burke, Tariro Blessing Makeyi, Munyaradzi Masaka, Bridget Parere, Clever Muringi, Fortune Munyonga, Romeo Kambanga, Xoliso Sithole, Melbar Dick, Hatirarame Jenatry Muranganwa (Chihota), Ella Chirunga, Patson Muzuwa, Regina Vengai and many not mentioned. They were not gathered in a political meeting hall in Bulawayo or Masvingo.
Perhaps one of the most beautiful aspects of the gathering was the welcome extended to the young people by members of the local community. The youths were received with generosity and practical assistance. Community members provided chairs, charcoal and other basic necessities, helping to make the gathering possible. Such gestures may appear modest, but they carry enormous meaning. A chair may simply be a chair. A bag of charcoal may simply be charcoal. This made them feel at home away from Zimbabwe. But when offered to young people who are thousands of miles from their homeland, these simple acts become expressions of community, solidarity and hospitality. They demonstrate that diaspora activism does not have to exist in isolation. It can become part of the wider social fabric of the community in which Zimbabweans now live.
The Durham meeting therefore became more than a CDF gathering. It was also an example of how communities can come together across nationality, background and political differences. There was also something almost poetic about discussing constitutional power in the Land of the Prince Bishops. Durham’s history is deeply connected to questions of power, authority, faith and governance. The city developed around the shrine of St Cuthbert, while its medieval Prince Bishops exercised extraordinary spiritual and secular authority. Durham Castle and Durham Cathedral remain part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site and dominate the city’s remarkable landscape.
The official Durham tourism authority describes the city as the “Land of the Prince Bishops”, recalling a period when Durham’s bishops possessed powers that extended far beyond purely religious responsibilities. Against this historic backdrop, young Zimbabweans discussing constitutional power, accountability and the relationship between citizens and government created an interesting historical contrast. The lesson from history is that power is never permanent. Institutions evolve.
Societies change. And ultimately, legitimate authority must remain accountable to the people. The most serious issue discussed by the youths was Constitutional Amendment No. 3, commonly known as CAB3. It is important to distinguish between the Government’s justification for the amendment and the objections raised by civil-society and constitutional-rights groups.
The Government presented CAB3 as a package of reforms intended to modernise Zimbabwe’s constitutional framework, strengthen governance and provide greater institutional stability. But youths have focused particularly on changes affecting the presidency, Parliament and the constitutional relationship between voters and their representatives. The original CAB3 proposal included a fundamental change to the way the President would be chosen: instead of being directly elected by Zimbabwean voters, the President would be elected by Parliament. The proposal also sought to extend the presidential and parliamentary terms from five years to seven years, with the extension applying to the incumbent office-holders. The initial proposal would therefore have moved the next general election from 2028 to 2030.
For CDF and other critics, this is not merely a technical constitutional adjustment. It goes to the heart of the principle that political power belongs to the people. Hence the youth will alert the international world of the corrupt way staying in power. Under the amendment, the President would be elected by members of the Senate and National Assembly sitting jointly. The candidate would need more than half of the valid parliamentary votes, with a run-off between the two leading candidates if no candidate achieved a majority in the first ballot.
Youths argued that such a system can weaken the direct electoral relationship between citizens and the Head of State. It could mean that the ordinary voter no longer casts a direct vote for President. For youths, the problem is not simply whether seven years is better or worse than five years. The deeper question is who benefits from the amendment and when it takes effect. Changing the rules for future governments is one constitutional question that the youths want to keep alive. This is precisely why the Law Society of Zimbabwe expressed serious concern about applying the extension to current office holders, even while regarding some other aspects of the Bill as not legally problematic in themselves.
Zimbabwe’s Constitution contains special procedures for constitutional amendments. Section 328 provides enhanced safeguards for certain amendments, including provisions affecting presidential and parliamentary terms. Veritas has taken the position that because CAB3 purported to extend the terms beyond the constitutional maximums and apply the extensions to incumbents, a national referendum was required before the amendment could be submitted for presidential assent.
According to Veritas, CAB3 was nevertheless signed and published as an Act on 7 July 2026 without such a referendum. Veritas consequently argues that the purported enactment is constitutionally defective and that the Act is not properly in force. The CDF youths takes the same position and strengthening their resolve to keep the conversation going on. It is about the constitutional inheritance they believe they are entitled to receive when they return home.
Some may ask why Zimbabweans living in Britain, South Africa, Australia, America or elsewhere should be concerned about constitutional amendments taking place in Zimbabwe. Citizenship does not end at the airport. The Zimbabwean diaspora remains economically, socially and emotionally connected to Zimbabwe. Millions of Zimbabweans live outside the country or have family members abroad. They send money home, support relatives, invest in businesses, maintain homes, participate in community organisations and remain involved in national debates.
Yet one of the unresolved questions in Zimbabwe remains the political participation of citizens in the diaspora. Zimbabweans living abroad can have profound economic and family connections to the country, yet their ability to participate directly in national elections remains restricted. Therefore, when constitutional changes alter the method of electing the President or change the duration of Parliament, the consequences are not necessarily confined to people physically inside Zimbabwe.
The diaspora is affected because it is part of the Zimbabwean nation. For Zimbabweans demonstrating peacefully in Britain, CAB3 provides another constitutional issue around which diaspora groups can organise, campaign and raise awareness. But there is an important distinction. The passage of CAB3 does not, by itself, make peaceful demonstrations by Zimbabweans abroad unlawful, but it can criminalise them as they are working with foreigners to highlight the plight of ordinary Zimbabweans which can be perceived as damaging the image of the country through the Criminal Law and Codification Act 2023.
Zimbabwean constitutional changes cannot simply turn a peaceful protest in Durham, London, Manchester or Birmingham into a criminal offence under British law. However, diaspora activists may be concerned about the consequences of their activism when they travel to Zimbabwe or interact with Zimbabwean authorities.
As previously written by the Zanu-PF member Dr. Masimba Mavaza as gathering of traitors. This is good enough to change the narrative and lead into arrests as they will be seen to be damaging the sovereignty of the country especially coming from a trusted member of their party who represents in the diaspora. That is why the constitutional debate has significance beyond Zimbabwe’s borders.
A person standing in Durham holding a placard about constitutional democracy is exercising political expression in the United Kingdom. The British people support means they will ask their MP’s to table motions in parliament. It was a message of peaceful constitutional engagement. They want to see constitutional questions debated openly and democratically. That is why the gathering’s emphasis on hope is important. The youths did not present themselves as people who had abandoned Zimbabwe. They presented themselves as Zimbabweans who still believed Zimbabwe could change.
The young people also deserve recognition for the discipline and determination demonstrated in organising the Durham meeting. But youth activism cannot flourish without leadership and support. Special appreciation therefore goes to the CDF leadership in the United Kingdom for permitting, encouraging and supporting the young people to participate in this important gathering.
Particular recognition should go to CDF Chairlady Tariro Blessing Makeyi, Fortune Munyonga and Stanford Biti, alongside other leaders and supporters who stood with the youth. Their support illustrates an important principle: the future of any democratic movement ultimately depends on its ability to encourage young people to participate rather than merely speak on their behalf. The involvement of younger Zimbabweans ensures that constitutional debate is not left exclusively to an older generation.
A special word of appreciation should also go to John Burke, who was present with the youths even though his primary purpose in Durham was connected with ZHRO business. His presence nevertheless demonstrated solidarity. Sometimes support does not require a formal speech. Sometimes simply being there matters.
For young people engaged in a difficult and emotionally demanding discussion about their homeland, seeing community leaders and established activists standing beside them can provide encouragement. There was another layer of symbolism to the gathering. It coincided with the birthday of Patson Muzuwa. Birthdays are traditionally moments of looking backwards and forwards remembering the journey already travelled while looking towards the future.
For a Zimbabwean diaspora activist, that future is inevitably connected to the country from which the journey began. The birthday therefore became more than a 60 year personal celebration. It became an occasion around which young Zimbabweans could celebrate friendship, community and their continued attachment to Zimbabwe.
There is something fitting about young Zimbabweans meeting in a city whose history reminds visitors that power, institutions and political authority change over time. They met openly unlike in Zimbabwe where you need police clearance to meet as a group like that and sometimes be dispersed by riot police. In this case they were in open and having full support of the police, fire brigade and community.
It demonstrates that young Zimbabweans abroad remain interested in the political and constitutional direction of their homeland.
It demonstrates that community support can sustain activism even far from home. It demonstrates that constitutional debate can take place peacefully across borders.
And it demonstrates that patriotism does not necessarily require physical presence in Zimbabwe. The CDF youths travelled, gathered, talked, laughed and celebrated a 60th birthday but they also carried a serious constitutional message. They want a Zimbabwe in which the Constitution belongs to the people rather than political office holders.

title: Cuatro pioneras ginecólogas catalanas
content:
Cuatro pioneras ginecólogas catalanas
Lectores Expertos
Dolors Aleu i Riera se convirtió en el año 1882 en la primera mujer licenciada en Medicina en España
* El autor forma parte de la comunidad de lectores de La Vanguardia
El siglo XIX marcó el acceso de las primeras mujeres a los estudios universitarios en España. Las pioneras de la medicina catalana encontraron en la ginecología y la pediatría sus espacios naturales de ejercicio profesional.
El nacimiento de la Pediatría como especialidad surge en España a finales del siglo XIX. Hasta entonces se englobaba dentro de la especialidad de Obstetricia, enfermedades de los niños y mujeres.
1. Dolors Aleu i Riera
Nacida en Barcelona (7 de abril de 1857 - 18 de febrero de 1913), se convirtió en 1882 en la primera mujer licenciada en Medicina en España. Se matriculó en la Universitat de Barcelona en 1874. Terminó sus estudios con una calificación excelente en 1879, pero las trabas burocráticas del gobierno retrasaron su examen de grado oficial hasta 1882.
Se convirtió en la segunda mujer del país en obtener el título de doctora, defendiendo en Madrid su tesis “De la necesidad de encaminar por una nueva senda la educación higiénico-moral de la mujer (1883). El texto original, que fue publicado formalmente en Barcelona en 1883, constituyó una defensa pionera de los derechos de las mujeres.
Ejerció de forma muy activa durante más de 25 años en su propia consulta en Barcelona, especializándose en ginecología y pediatría. Fue profesora de Higiene Doméstica en la Academia de Ciencias, Artes y Oficios para la mujer, fundada el 2 de mayo de 1885 en el número 10 de la Rambla de Canaletes por la artista y concertista Clotilde Cerdà y Bosch (conocida como Esmeralda Cervantes), con el propósito de promover la emancipación y la educación superior y profesional de las mujeres. Fue un centro pionero en España para dar acceso a la formación técnica, científica y artística a la mujer en el siglo XIX.
Fue una firme defensora de los derechos de la mujer y de la salud femenina, llegando a criticar públicamente el uso del corsé de la época por los problemas médicos que causaba.
Dolors Aleu es recordada con el nombre Centre Sociosanitari Putget Dolors Aleu, actualmente denominado Hospital d'Atenció Intermèdia Colisée Barcelona Dolors Aleu.
La Universidad de Barcelona dio el nombre de Dolors Aleu a un aula de la Facultad de Medicina y Ciencias de la Salud.
2. Trinitat Sais i Plaja
Fue una de las médicas pioneras de España, nacida a finales del siglo XIX y con una destacada trayectoria en ginecología y pediatría.
Nació el 22 de julio de 1878 en La Bisbal de l'Empordà (Girona). Falleció el 17 de octubre de 1933 en Barcelona. Era hija de una comadrona y un sastre, lo que muy probablemente despertó su temprana vocación por la salud de las mujeres y los nacimientos.
Fue la octaba mujer en estudiar Medicina en Catalunya y la primera mujer médica de la provincia de Girona.
Estudió magisterio y obtuvo el título en Barcelona en 1893. Posteriormente estudió el bachillerato en el Instituto de Figueras y obtuvo el premio extraordinario en 1896. Siguió despues estudios de Medicina en la universidad de Barcelona donde se licenció en 1903
Tras graduarse en 1903, la Dra. Sais desarrolló una intensa labor profesional enfocada principalmente en la salud materno-infantil, un campo donde las mujeres médicas de la época encontraron un espacio fundamental para ejercer.
Participó en la organización de diversos congresos como el primer congreso Español de la Tuberculosis en la que fue vicepresidenta del Comité de Damas.
Tuvo sus principales consultas médicas en la calle de Pelayo y posteriormente en la calle de Bergara, anunciando sus servicios para la atención de “mujeres y niños”. Más tarde también ejerció como pediatra y tocóloga (obstetra) en el barrio de Sant Gervasi.
Divulgó sus conocimientos científicos mediante conferencias y cursos en los que también defendía los derechos de la mujer en revistas como como La mujer moderna en Manresa y Feminal .
En 1914 fue la primera mujer en impartir la conferencia de apertura de curso en el Colegio Oficial de Médicos de Barcelona, donde cuestionó la falta de formación de las mujeres en puericultura, y la falta de higiene como primera causa de mortalidad infantil. Sus hijas, Teresa y Edelmira, también fueron médicas.
3. Francesca Fontova i Rosell
Francesca Fontova i Rosell (Lleida, 31 d'octubre de 1877 – Avilés, Astúries, 25 d'agost de 1961). Fue la primera mujer licenciada en Medicina en la provincia de Lleida y una de las pioneras de la Medicina en la Cataluña de finales del siglo XIX y principios del XX.
Estudió Magisterio y obtuvo el título de bachiller en Artes por el Instituto de Lleida el 1895. Intentó ingresar en la Facultad de Medicina de la Universidad de Barcelona. Sin embargo, una circular oficial de 1893 prohibía el acceso de las mujeres a la educación superior.
Solicitó una autorización directamente al Ministerio de Instrucción Pública, el cual le concedió el permiso definitivo en 1898, cinco años después.
Se licenció en Medicina en 1903. Formó parte de una promoción histórica de pioneras junto a Trinitat Sais y Miracle Andreu (quienes sí se volcaron más directamente en la Ginecología y la Tocología).
Inicialmente ejerció en Lleida y en varios municipios de la comarca del Segrià. En 1906, tras contraer matrimonio con el también médico Miquel Real, se trasladó al barrio de Gràcia en Barcelona. Allí colaboró activamente en la clínica de su esposo, asumiendo tareas médicas generales, quirúrgicas y de anestesia.
En Barcelona, ejercieron dos hijas farmacéuticas, Paquita y Teresa Real Fontova y también un hijo médico Miquel Real Fontova.
4. Maria Lluïsa Quadras Bordes
Maria Lluïsa Quadras Bordes nació el 28 de junio de 1898 en Barcelona. Era hija de Joan Quadras Vidal, un comerciante, y de Agnès Bordes Casal. Maria Lluïsa estudió Medicina. Empezó la carrera en Barcelona, más adelante se mudó a Zaragoza y, finalmente, realizó el último curso en Valencia.
Obtuvo su licenciatura en 1920 y se especializó en Ginecología. Un año después de finalizar la carrera abrió su propia consulta. Fue una Ginecóloga con gran implicación en la actividad benéfica.
Abrió su primera consulta especializada en Barcelona en octubre de 1921 en la calle de Santa Anna, y meses más tarde trasladó y amplió su centro médico al número 127 de la calle Mallorca. La prensa de Barcelona la dio a conocer como la primera mujer radióloga y abrió el Instituto de Electrología, Radiología y Ginecología, un centro que también atendía a las mujeres sin recursos económicos.
Realizó numerosos viajes de formación profesional , principalmente a Francia, en los que visitaba centros médicos para completar su formación .
En 1931, su hermana Maria Victòria terminó la carrera de Medicina y empezó a trabajar con ella en la consulta y tuvieron su consulta abierta hasta 1984.
La doctora Quadras trabajó también en el Hospital Sant Pau y en el Hospital Clínic. Fue socia de la Academia y Laboratorio de Ciencias Médicas, de la Academia de Higiene de Catalunya, socia honorífica de la Sociedad Francesa de Gi necología y miembro de la Catalana de Ginecología y Obstetricia.
Tuvo un papel esencial en la fundaciónde la Asociación contra la Toxicomanía, que se constituyó en el Colegio de Médicos de Barcelona en 1926.
Fundó una entidad llamada El abrigo de los pobres, cuya finalidad era ofrecer ropa y elementos para el hogar a las personas más necesitadas y a los hospitales. Maria Lluïsa Quadras Bordes falleció el 10 de septiembre de 1989 en Barcelona.

title: Bộ Y tế phát động Chương trình quốc gia về bảo vệ trẻ em
content:
Nhiều nguy cơ mới trên môi trường mạng
Phát biểu tại lễ phát động, Thứ trưởng Bộ Y tế Lê Đức Luận cho biết công tác bảo vệ trẻ em thời gian qua đã đạt được nhiều kết quả đáng ghi nhận.
Tỉ lệ trẻ em lao động trái quy định của pháp luật đã giảm từ 5,4% còn 1,31%. 100% trẻ em bị xâm hại được áp dụng các biện pháp hỗ trợ, can thiệp phù hợp. Hệ thống dịch vụ bảo vệ trẻ em được tổ chức theo ba cấp độ gồm phòng ngừa, hỗ trợ và can thiệp.
Tổng đài điện thoại quốc gia bảo vệ trẻ em 111 tiếp tục là địa chỉ tiếp nhận thông tin, tư vấn và phối hợp xử lý các vụ việc liên quan đến quyền trẻ em. Việt Nam cũng đã chính thức khai trương Tổng đài phòng, chống bạo lực gia đình 117.
Tuy nhiên theo ông Luận, công tác bảo vệ trẻ em vẫn đứng trước nhiều khó khăn, thách thức. Tình trạng bạo lực trẻ em có xu hướng gia tăng trên phạm vi toàn cầu trong bối cảnh suy thoái kinh tế, lạm phát và những cú sốc từ thiên tai, xã hội. Đây là những yếu tố khiến trẻ em yếu thế có nguy cơ bỏ học và tham gia lao động sớm.
Lao động trẻ em vẫn tồn tại tại khu vực nông, lâm, thủy sản, trong các hộ gia đình và cơ sở sản xuất, kinh doanh nhỏ lẻ - những nơi khó kiểm tra, giám sát.
Trong khi đó mạng lưới cung cấp dịch vụ bảo vệ trẻ em tại một số địa phương còn mỏng, việc kết nối, liên thông và chuyển tuyến dịch vụ chưa đồng bộ.
Đặc biệt, các nguy cơ đối với trẻ em không chỉ diễn ra trong đời sống thực, mà ngày càng mở rộng sang môi trường mạng.
Bà Michaela Bauer, Phó trưởng đại diện UNICEF tại Việt Nam, cho biết trẻ em tại Việt Nam vẫn phải đối mặt với nhiều nguy cơ như bạo lực, bóc lột, xâm hại tình dục, trong đó có xâm hại và bóc lột trên môi trường mạng, cùng nguy cơ phải làm những công việc nặng nhọc, độc hại.
Theo bà Michaela Bauer, để giải quyết những thách thức này, chỉ hoàn thiện luật pháp và chính sách là chưa đủ. Việt Nam cần một hệ thống bảo vệ trẻ em vững mạnh, tích hợp và được bảo đảm nguồn lực tài chính.
Hệ thống này cần đội ngũ nhân viên công tác xã hội có năng lực, dữ liệu tin cậy, cơ chế phối hợp hiệu quả và các dịch vụ bảo vệ trẻ em có thể tiếp cận tại mọi cộng đồng.
"Các bằng chứng quốc tế cho thấy trẻ em được bảo vệ tốt nhất khi công tác phòng ngừa và ứng phó được triển khai như một hệ thống thống nhất, xuyên suốt từ cấp quốc gia đến gia đình, nhà trường và cộng đồng", bà Michaela Bauer nhấn mạnh.
Phấn đấu giảm 5% trẻ em bị bạo lực, xâm hại mỗi năm
Chương trình quốc gia về bảo vệ trẻ em và phòng ngừa, giảm thiểu trẻ em lao động trái quy định của pháp luật giai đoạn 2026 - 2030 đặt ra nhiều mục tiêu đến năm 2030.
Theo đó tỉ lệ trẻ em bị bạo lực và xâm hại tình dục sẽ giảm ít nhất 5% mỗi năm. Tỉ lệ lao động trẻ em trong độ tuổi từ 5 đến 17 tuổi được đặt mục tiêu giảm xuống dưới 1,1%.
Đặc biệt, chương trình hướng đến tăng cường quản lý, kết nối dữ liệu để kịp thời nhận diện và hỗ trợ trẻ em có nguy cơ.
Theo mục tiêu đề ra, 100% trẻ em thuộc đối tượng bảo vệ và trẻ em có nguy cơ sẽ được quản lý trên hệ thống cơ sở dữ liệu trẻ em, kết nối dùng chung với các cơ sở dữ liệu liên quan.
Việc xây dựng hệ thống dữ liệu và tăng cường kết nối giữa các cơ quan, đơn vị được kỳ vọng giúp công tác bảo vệ trẻ em chuyển mạnh từ xử lý khi vụ việc xảy ra sang chủ động phòng ngừa, phát hiện sớm và can thiệp kịp thời.

title: A.P. NGO welcomes UN’s declaration of November 27 as Global Day Against Child Marriage
content:
The UN declaration of November 27 as Global Day Against Child Marriages is an international recognition of the sustained efforts of organisations like Just Rights for Children (JRC), said B. Keerthy, president of the Vijayawada-based Vasavya Mahila Mandali (VMM). JRC is an NGO network working with governments and enforcement agencies to prevent child marriages across the country.
Speaking at a media conference on Sunday (September 6, 2026), Ms. Keerthy said VMM was a partner in JRC’s long-running campaign seeking a dedicated international day against child marriage and had been engaged in grassroots campaign against child marriages in NTR and Krishna districts. She welcomed the UN’s historic declaration, which was a matter of pride for India where the Government had launched the Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat (Child Marriage-Free India) campaign with JRC partners on November 27, 2024.
“An international commitment must now be translated into action at the grassroots level,” she said and stressed that the fight would remain incomplete as long as even a single child remained at risk of child marriage. She said VMM had undertaken awareness programmes in schools, panchayats, and villages, encouraged communities to take anti-child marriage pledges, linked vulnerable families with government welfare schemes and worked to bring school dropouts back into education system. Through legal intervention, VMM had prevented 2,175 child marriages in NTR and Krishna districts, she said.
She said the JRC founder Bhuvan Ribhu had launched the international campaign for a dedicated global day to end child marriage. In March 2026, he reiterated the call for a UN resolution in the presence of international leaders, including Sierra Leone’s First Lady Dr Fatima Maada Bio, who supported the initiative. Sierra Leone subsequently led the effort at the UN General Assembly, with support from around 67 countries, including India. The resolution was adopted on September 4.
JRC’s Andhra Pradesh State coordinator B. Chandrasekhar said the organisation, in collaboration with partner organisations, worked with governments across 782 districts in India, mobilising communities, schools, panchayats, women, police, religious leaders and political representatives. The collective effort had helped prevent more than 5.5 lakh child marriages, he said.

title: In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
url: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
content:
In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
SHANGHAI – At the Sept. 19 Shanghai premiere of her feature debut, “Shanghai Daughter,” Shen Zhongmin carried a rubber seed from the forests of the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture, nearly 3,000 kilometers away in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, where her late father had worked.
“The seed fell from the canopy and struck me as I retraced his life there,” Shen, 41, tells Sixth Tone.
Her father was among the millions of urban Chinese youths “sent down” to work in rural areas under the Down to the Countryside Movement, a campaign that ran from the mid-1950s through the late 1970s. He spent a decade on a state-run rubber farm near China’s border with Myanmar but rarely spoke to his daughter about those years.
Shen, who works professionally as Agnis Shen, first traveled to Xishuangbanna in 2011, the year after her father died. A former culture editor at the Shanghai-based magazine The Bund and the author of “The Traveler’s Desire,” a collection of short fiction. She returned to the region repeatedly, retracing her father’s life and meeting people from his generation.
Nearly a decade after her first trip, those encounters and widespread coverage of a herd of wild Asian elephants wandering north from Xishuangbanna helped inspire the idea for a film. The herd’s journey drew attention to the rubber plantations that had transformed parts of the region’s rainforest habitat.
Blending fiction with documentary methods, “Shanghai Daughter” follows Ming, a fictional Shanghai woman played by Liang Cuishan, as she seeks out her father’s former acquaintances in Xishuangbanna.
She encounters workers’ dormitories facing demolition and a landscape where mining and modern agriculture are replacing former rubber plantations. She also meets rubber tappers, village doctors, ethnic Dai villagers, and ecological researchers, all of whom appear as themselves and recount their own experiences.
“The film asks how we deal with memory,” Shen says. “When you want to understand something from the past but cannot find reliable firsthand records, how do you search for the answers?”
“Shanghai Daughter” had its world premiere in the Panorama section of the Berlin International Film Festival in February and was later selected for the Hong Kong International Film Festival and the Malaysia International Film Festival.
Seven months later, the film’s Shanghai premiere drew at least a dozen former sent-down youths from the city, all now in their 70s. They traveled about an hour by subway to attend.
At the theater, they shared old photographs from their years in Xishuangbanna, including images taken with Shen’s father, Shen Wanxiong, and posed for a group photo with the director.
Among them was Shen Weilong, 73, a former rubber tapper who had worked alongside Shen Wanxiong and describes him as his best friend. Looking at one of the photographs, he jokes, “This one doesn’t show just how handsome he was. If you want to know what he looked like, just look at his daughter.”
As he speaks about his generation, tears well in his eyes. “Our generation is rarely talked about, and now our time is running out,” he says.
Sixth Tone spoke with Shen Zhongmin the following day as she continued a multi-city promotional tour. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.
Sixth Tone: Not a single scene in “Shanghai Daughter” was shot in Shanghai. Why did you choose the title, and what does it mean to you?
Shen: “Shanghai daughters” was originally a local term. Villagers near the farms used it for daughters left behind by sent-down youths. Over time, the label seemed to replace each woman’s real name.
Because of my father’s history, I am also, in a sense, a “Shanghai daughter,” and so I went there too. In Xishuangbanna, the phrase took on a double meaning for me. It suggested a kind of twin existence, like looking in a mirror. We seemed to have completely different yet intersecting destinies, one born in Shanghai and the other 3,000 kilometers away in Xishuangbanna.
To me, “daughter” carries something different from either “woman” or “boy.” One of the first Dai expressions my father taught me was “long yin,” meaning “girl.” The image of a girl carries a particular gentleness that can help heal or ease the deep wounds and heaviness behind this subject. The emotional connection extends beyond father and daughter to one girl and another, and one daughter and another.
I did not want to remain trapped within a particular historical wound or view that period only through criticism. I hoped to create something relevant to the present and oriented toward the future, an expression of repair, renewed empathy, and hope.
Sixth Tone: By telling the story from a daughter’s perspective, the film approaches the sent-down youth movement through one family. How does that perspective differ from other portrayals of the movement?
Shen: This is a deeply personal and highly artistic undertaking. It emphasizes experiencing and observing our surroundings and sensory world anew.
While writing the screenplay, I did extensive research. I gathered oral histories, consulted historical archives, and reconnected with researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who study rainforest restoration. But I wanted to hold back those “concrete” materials for as long as possible and put perception first. Thoughts and opinions can easily create divisions, and once expressed, they have their limits. Perception, however, can be shared and remains more open.
Later, an academically minded journalist asked whether this might be related to ecofeminism. I thought the observation was perceptive. It points toward a perspective that moves beyond anthropocentrism and rejects a structure in which “I am the center, and everyone else is the other.”
Sixth Tone: Rubber trees, dragon fruit, and other elements of the landscape recur throughout the film. How did you use them to connect personal memory with the region’s history?
Shen: During my fieldwork in Xishuangbanna, I often walked around whenever I had time. I gradually came to see the landscape itself as a theater. All the legends and stories I had heard, with their intense dramatic and emotional tension, lay silently buried in a small hill in the village.
Generations have cultivated different crops there, from rice and corn to bananas and, more recently, dragon fruit. A small patch of primary forest protected by the Dai people remains on the hillside. Beneath the present landscape lie my father’s old dormitory and the former rubber plantation.
People disappear faster than memories, but stories spanning more than half a century survive in the land’s subtle traces. When you look at the plants and the land and listen to their voices, it feels as if they are telling you stories, though not in a language humans can hear.
I brought the rubber seed to the screening because, to me, it represents a transformation of cause and effect. More than half a century ago, people had little choice but to clear primary rainforest and plant rubber trees to meet the needs of national development. We now understand that this harmed local biodiversity.
A Chinese Academy of Sciences team is rehabilitating degraded rubber groves. Its goal is not to return them to primary rainforest, which would be scientifically unsound, but to rebalance relationships among species. The researchers are restoring poor-quality groves left by haphazard planting and tapping and introducing species that can bridge rubber plantations and native tropical rainforest. By giving the rubber trees a range of “good neighbors,” they can gradually restore the ecosystem’s layers.
To me, they are taking the “effect” of an earlier decision and planting within it a new, positive “cause,” one that may bear better fruit in the future. The relationship between seed and fruit becomes a metaphor for the transformation of cause and effect. I find that deeply inspiring.
Making the film also took me to Malaysia, where I saw some of the country’s earliest rubber trees. Without that initial transplantation, rubber would not have been planted on such a large scale in Xishuangbanna, and many of these stories would not exist.
Sixth Tone: Why did you blend fiction and documentary methods rather than make a conventional documentary centered on your own search?
Shen: I have always felt that the boundary between reality and fiction is unclear, much like the line between dreams and waking life. Historical narratives also have a dreamlike quality for me, something I have explored in my fiction.
If I had relied on documentary methods alone to examine the sent-down youth movement or my relationship with my father, the film would have felt too narrow.
I drew on my own experience to present subjects I have long cared about in a more contemporary, open form. If I had appeared as myself and made a pure documentary, the film would have become too narrow, confined by the standards of historical fact and leaving viewers less room to project themselves into it and experience it openly.
Sixth Tone: How did you approach your father’s past and his former co-workers while making the film? How did they respond after the premiere?
Shen: My father rarely spoke about the decade he spent in Xishuangbanna. People of his generation generally do not talk about those experiences.
You could sense a deep wound behind the way an older audience member spoke yesterday. At times, his questions seemed to judge other people, but they ultimately revealed his own views and emotions.
I didn’t even know my father had tapped rubber. He had never told me what work he did there. Only when I first walked into the plantation did I understand that these were rubber trees and that his generation had planted and tapped them.
At first, I avoided contacting my father’s former co-workers. I knew they would be eager to help and provide a great deal of firsthand material. But the film began with the particular relationship between my father and me. He had told me very little and died before I could learn more, so I went there to search for and reconstruct that missing part of his life.
I also did not want to disturb them for what was, after all, a small personal project. Revisiting those experiences can be extremely painful, especially for some of them.
Since yesterday’s premiere, I have spent all morning replying to their messages. Today, they are gathering for a reunion lunch to discuss the film.
One of my father’s former co-workers wrote: “Thank you to the screenwriter, creative team, and director for bringing a fitting close to our 50 years as sent-down youths.”
Editor: Apurva.
