title: A los 84 años sigue trabajando en el campo: la historia de Malena Sanguinetti
content:
La inauguración de la 121ª Expo Rural del Prado tuvo un momento especialmente dedicado a quienes han construido su vínculo con el campo desde lugares muy diferentes. Bajo la consigna “Las Rurales”, la Asociación Rural del Uruguay (ARU) reconoció tres mujeres con historias atravesadas por el trabajo, la producción, la vocación y, sobre todo, la perseverancia.
Las homenajeadas fueron Malena Sanguinetti Ponce de León, Marisa Viera e Isabel Chiarino, y, a su vez, se reconoció la trayectoria del médico veterinario Jaime Castells. Cuatro recorridos distintos, desde generaciones y realidades también diferentes, pero unidos por una vida estrechamente vinculada al medio rural.
Malena Sanguinetti: a los 84 años, sigue al frente del campo
Malena Sanguinetti Ponce de León tiene 84 años y continúa trabajando en el campo familiar en Canelones, a pocos minutos de Montevideo. La historia del establecimiento se remonta a 1907, cuando la tierra fue adquirida por su abuelo, mientras que su padre comenzó a trabajarla tres décadas después.
Pero su propia historia productiva también tiene mucho para contar. A los 70 años, con un campo que mostraba señales de desgaste, encontró nuevas herramientas para transformar el sistema y seguir adelante.
En 62 hectáreas desarrolló un esquema de pastoreo con 70 potreros, con agua y sombra en cada parcela. También buscó mejorar el tipo de ganado, trabajando con animales de tamaño moderado y genética Red Angus. El sistema, además de mejorar la utilización del campo, terminó siendo una herramienta para que pudiera continuar trabajando a una edad en la que muchos ya se han retirado.
Su historia estuvo marcada por aprender haciendo. Malena contó que le hubiera gustado continuar estudiando, pero las circunstancias de la vida no se lo permitieron. Eso, sin embargo, nunca significó dejar de formarse.
“Nunca dejé de aprender a través del trabajo y la experiencia”, expresó. Con esfuerzo, responsabilidad y compromiso, sostuvo, siempre buscó salir adelante y darle lo mejor a su familia.
Incluso dudó antes de aceptar el reconocimiento. Finalmente estuvo en el Prado para recibirlo y convertirse, a sus 84 años, en una de las protagonistas de la inauguración.
Cuatro historias diferentes. Una productora que sigue trabajando a los 84 años; una mujer que encontró en el tambo una oportunidad y hoy lidera un equipo; una cabañera que debió abrirse camino en un ámbito que inicialmente le habían dicho que no era para ella; y un veterinario que después de más de seis décadas de profesión sigue entendiendo el trabajo como una forma de servir a los demás.
Cuatro historias con las que la Rural del Prado eligió, en el comienzo de su 121ª edición, reconocer también a muchas otras que se repiten todos los días en el campo uruguayo.

title: Food security is a global security imperative
content:
Recent disruptions—from extreme weather events to geopolitical tensions affecting international trade—have underscored a fundamental reality: no nation, regardless of its wealth or geography, can secure its food future alone.
Building resilient food systems requires far more than increasing agricultural output. It requires open and reliable trade, secure maritime routes, scientific innovation, sustainable water management, and strong international partnerships.
Together, these elements place food security at the intersection of economic resilience, sustainable development, and global stability.
These realities have shaped the United Arab Emirates' approach to food security. Despite its arid climate, water scarcity, and limited arable land, the UAE has treated food security as a strategic national resilience priority – one that extends well beyond agricultural production.
Through the National Food Security Strategy 2051, the country is strengthening food resilience by diversifying international supply sources, facilitating reliable food trade, expanding sustainable domestic production, strengthening strategic preparedness, reducing food loss and waste, and developing supply chains capable of withstanding future shocks.
Innovation is central to this vision. The UAE continues to invest in controlled-environment agriculture, hydroponics, vertical farming, precision irrigation, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and other climate-smart agricultural solutions.
UAE-based companies are developing large-scale vertical farms that produce fresh produce in controlled environments while using significantly less water and land than conventional agriculture. These technologies can increase productivity while easing pressure on scarce water resources.
This transformation is not only about technology. Through initiatives led by the National Agriculture Centre and programmes supporting young and female farmers, the UAE is building national capabilities, fostering agricultural entrepreneurship, and strengthening the human capital needed for a competitive and future-ready food economy.
This approach also reflects a broader economic vision. Through the UAE Food Cluster Strategy, the country is connecting agriculture with advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, food processing, logistics, and research to build a more integrated and competitive food ecosystem.
The 2026 Emirates Agriculture Conference and Exhibition brought together farmers, industry, investors, researchers, and government across the food value chain, reflecting an approach that sees food security not only as a resilience priority, but also as a driver of innovation, investment, skilled employment, and economic diversification.
The UAE’s experience also reflects a wider reality: national resilience depends on the resilience of the global food system. Modern agriculture relies on uninterrupted access to fertilizers, seeds, animal feed, energy, and efficient global logistics networks.
Disruptions to maritime routes or supply chains can quickly affect food availability, drive up prices, and threaten the livelihoods of millions—particularly in countries that depend heavily on imported food. Safeguarding the continuity of these flows is therefore not only an economic necessity; it is a humanitarian responsibility.
Nowhere is this interdependence more evident than in the Strait of Hormuz. This vital international waterway is a global lifeline, carrying approximately one-fifth of global energy supplies and around 30 per cent of the fertilizers essential to global food production.
Any disruption to such a critical artery is therefore not a regional concern alone. Its effects can reverberate through global markets and supply chains, with the greatest consequences often falling on vulnerable, food-import-dependent countries.
This wider responsibility has also shaped the UAE’s engagement through multilateral institutions. On 28 April 2026, the FAO Council adopted by consensus a UAE-led decision addressing the implications of supply chain disruptions in the Gulf region for global food security and agriculture.
The decision called for preventing the politicization of food and agricultural supply chains and strengthened the FAO’s role in monitoring disruptions, providing timely market information and early warnings, and supporting countries in building more resilient agri-food systems.
But resilience cannot be built through preparedness alone. We must also transform how food is produced, financed, and brought to the market, while confronting the growing pressures of climate change and resource scarcity.
The UAE has advanced this agenda internationally by placing food systems at the heart of the global climate conversation.
COP28 marked an important shift: for the first time, food and agriculture were given a prominent place within the climate agenda, reinforced by the Emirates Declaration on Sustainable Agriculture, Resilient Food Systems, and Climate Action.
Endorsed by 159 Heads of State and Government, the Declaration reflected a growing recognition that climate action cannot be separated from how the world produces, distributes, and consumes food.
COP28 also paired political ambition with practical investment, including the USD 200 million UAE–Gates Foundation partnership to accelerate agricultural innovation and strengthen the resilience of smallholder farmers in the Global South.
COP28’s broader legacy was equally significant. Hosted by the UAE, the conference brought 198 Parties together to agree on the landmark UAE Consensus, setting out an ambitious climate agenda to keep the 1.5°C goal within reach.
The Consensus provided an ambitious response to the Global Stocktake and a clear plan to close critical gaps by 2030.
It called on Parties to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems to reach net zero, encouraged economy-wide Nationally Determined Contributions, and set a new target to triple renewable energy capacity and double energy efficiency by 2030.
It also built momentum behind a new architecture for climate finance. The significance of this outcome extends beyond climate policy.
Aligned with the visionary leadership of the UAE, the COP28 Presidency marked a turning point in the effort to achieve tangible and essential progress on global climate action while advancing sustainable economic and social development.
It demonstrated the value of bringing countries together around practical solutions, shared ambition, and collective action.
That same emphasis on turning innovation into practical solutions is increasingly important across Asia. In 2026, the UAE contributed USD 1.5 million to an agricultural innovation fund administered by the Asian Development Bank to help scale proven technologies for farmers across Asia and the Pacific.
The initiative supports tools ranging from artificial intelligence and satellite monitoring to more efficient use of agricultural inputs, demonstrating how international partnerships can turn technological innovation into practical gains for farmers and food systems.
For the UAE and Indonesia, this agenda carries particular relevance.
Indonesia is among the countries in which these agricultural innovations are intended to be scaled, creating a practical foundation for our two countries to deepen cooperation in agricultural technology, investment, knowledge exchange, and resilient food systems.
As two countries deeply connected to international trade and regional supply chains, the UAE and Indonesia share a strong interest in ensuring that food systems remain productive, sustainable, and capable of adapting to future shocks.
No country possesses all the answers to today's complex food security challenges. Every country, however, has knowledge, innovation, and experience to contribute.
Governments, international organizations, research institutions, development partners, and the private sector each have a role to play – from strengthening agricultural resilience and safeguarding supply chains to ensuring that innovation reaches the communities that need it most.
The future of food security will therefore depend not simply on producing more food, but on building systems that can withstand and adapt to a more uncertain world.
That means using water and natural resources more responsibly, keeping global trade and supply chains open and reliable, investing in innovation, and strengthening cooperation across countries and sectors.
Ultimately, success must be measured by a simple test: whether food remains available, accessible, and affordable—particularly when shocks occur.
In an increasingly interconnected world, no nation can secure food security alone. It is a shared responsibility — one that demands sustained cooperation, practical action, and collective leadership.
*) Abdulla Salem AlDhaheri is Ambassador of the United Arab Emirates to the Republic of Indonesia and the Democratic Republic of Timor-Leste (Non-Resident)

title: With joy and grief, Palestinian football marks return
content:
With joy and grief, Palestinian football marks return
Palestinian sports commentator Khalil Jadallah has spent the past three years mourning the athletes killed in the Gaza war. As Palestinian football officially resumed this week, his return to the stadium proved bittersweet.
Palestinian professional sports were brought to a halt after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, in which 1,014 Palestinian athletes were killed, according to the Palestinian Football Association's tally.
On Friday, Jadallah was back at Faisal Al-Husseini Stadium in Al-Ram in the West Bank to call the opening match of the first tournament organised by the association in three years.
Though long awaited, the event was marked by contradicting emotions for Jadallah: "a feeling of joy at returning after such an absence, but also a feeling of loss. "
"We lost players... fans, administrators and referees," Jadallah told AFP.
- '1,000 Martyrs Cup' -
The football association named the comeback tournament -- which includes over 200 teams from the occupied West Bank, Gaza, and refugee camps in Lebanon -- the "1,000 Martyrs Cup".
Throughout the war, Palestinian football authorities have accused Israel of killing football players and damaging Gaza's sporting infrastructure.
Israel has said 12 Palestinian football figures that it killed in Gaza, including a FIFA-registered referee, were members of militant groups, an allegation the football association has rejected.
Large numbers of Palestinian security forces were deployed for the event, an unusual sight in the town more accustomed to Israeli military raids.
Before the game, pitting Jabal Al-Mukaber Club against Shabab Al-Khaleel SC, children carried a Palestinian flag wrapped to resemble a dead body, before unfurling it across the centre circle as a band played the Palestinian national anthem.
The sport authority also unveiled a memorial bearing the names of the killed Palestinian athletes outside the stadium, which stands in Al-Ram, not far from the West Bank separation barrier.
Samir Issa , a prominent former player and veteran manager who had coached both teams, watched from the stands as the game kicked off.
"Football has become more important than politics today," he said. "The proof of that is the following the World Cup has had."
"Sport in general is the culture of the people," he added, saying that Palestinians had "the right to practice sport normally and in all its forms, not just football".
At the 10-minute, 14-second mark, the referee ordered the game to stop for a minute of silence for the dead before the crowd grew loud again.
"Football returns to Palestine," read electronic screens around the stadium.
Thousands of mainly young people attended the game, with families, women and children seated in a separate section.
Maysan Suleiman, a 35-year-old from Al-Ram, said she came to commemorate "the martyrs".
- 'Football returns to Palestine' -
"I don't support either team," she said. "I came to support the idea (of the tournament) itself. After all, they're all sons of Palestine."
The tournament opened simultaneously in Gaza, where Israeli strikes have left much of the territory in ruins and some football fields have been turned into makeshift camps for those displaced by the war.
The opening match there was held in Deir al-Balah between Khadamat Rafah and Shabab Rafah as fans sat on plastic chairs around the small field lined with palm trees.
"Football represented life for us before the war, and after the war the lives of players stopped altogether," said Khalil Matar, a Khadamat Rafah player.
Matar said holding the cup simultaneously in the West Bank, Gaza and refugee camps in Lebanon reflected "national unity" for Palestinians.
But the West Bank teams are set to face major logistical hurdles as they travel between cities and Israeli military checkpoints in the occupied territory.
"Still, we're determined to continue sporting activities and developing our young people," said Abdullah Abu Ghassan of the Shabab Jaba team competing in the tournament.

title: WHO validates Chile as first South American country to eliminate dog-transmitted rabies
content:
Chile has become the first country in South America to eliminate dog-transmitted rabies to humans, following more than five decades of public health "prevention and surveillance," the World Health Organization said Monday.
The WHO said the last reported case of dog-to-human rabies occurred in 1972.
"This validation reflects decades of commitment to protecting communities from rabies and demonstrates the impact of sustained investment in public health," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a statement. "Chile's success offers valuable lessons for countries working to end human deaths caused by this preventable disease."
Rabies spreads through the saliva of an infected animal, usually through a bite. However, the virus can also infect someone if saliva enters the eyes, nose or mouth, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Rabies is almost always fatal once the initial symptoms appear, but it can be prevented through vaccination, effective surveillance and prompt access to post-exposure prophylaxis.
Chile has long maintained a public health policy focused on prevention and surveillance to combat the disease. Efforts include extensive vaccination campaigns for pets and vaccines for people who may have been exposed to the virus, WHO said. "These actions were complemented by door-to-door dog vaccination campaigns, specific measures for managing the dog population, and community awareness and education initiatives," it added.
Celebrating the milestone in Santiago, Chilean Health Minister May Chomali praised the " joint efforts " that led to the achievement.
"The public policy on rabies eradication has yielded the results we desired as a community and as a country," she said, highlighting the work inside communities and municipalities. "They are the ones on the ground, where education, vaccination, and pet control take place."
Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Director Jarbas Barbosa praised Chile for its role in demonstrating "what can be achieved" when countries invest in "vaccination, surveillance, and access to care."
Human cases of dog-transmitted rabies in the Americas have dropped by more than 98% since 1983, with only a few cases reported annually nowadays. That progress contrasts with the nearly 60,000 people killed by the virus every year, most bitten by dogs, according to WHO.

title: Al rescate de los waru waru, la técnica ancestral de cultivo que puede ser nuestra tecnología de punta frente a un cambio climático fuerte
content:
Al rescate de los waru waru, la técnica ancestral de cultivo que puede ser nuestra tecnología de punta frente a un cambio climático fuerte
Comunidades aimaras recuperan una milenaria técnica de cultivo sobre lagunas: un espectáculo visual y productivo que ha permitido recuperar variedades de papas nativas.
Este resumen es generado por inteligencia artificial y revisado por la redacción.
En Puno, sobre los 3.500 metros de altura, el inmenso altiplano parece un territorio indomable. Las heladas nocturnas, las sequías y el friaje hacen difícil la vida en esta región del país. Sin embargo, en los últimos meses, este panorama aparentemente inhóspito se ha transformado. Ante la vista, aparecen ahora enormes y perfectos paisajes circulares, de más de una hectárea de extensión. En el interior de estas tierras flotantes, rodeadas de canales de agua, crecen robustas papas nativas y productos como la quinua y la cañihua. Y en el exterior, habitan patos y otras aves migratorias, lo que genera un ecosistema de abono orgánico y natural.
Esta técnica de cultivo, conocida como waru waru, fue desarrollada desde épocas antiguas por las comunidades aimaras del altiplano, pero fue paulatinamente abandonada en el transcurso del siglo XX, ante la falta de recursos y mano de obra comunal, debido a la constante migración de las nuevas generaciones hacia las ciudades. Sin embargo, en el 2025, cuatro comunidades del distrito de Acora, con el apoyo de Cultivating Resilience, un programa de World Monuments Fund (WMF), que promueve la conservación de jardines históricos y paisajes culturales en el mundo, han podido recuperar estos cultivos ancestrales, producir las primeras cosechas, y ofrecer soluciones efectivas a los embates del cambio climático.
Campos agrícolas
“La organización, a través del programa Watch, recibe cada dos años postulaciones de sitios culturales de todo el mundo que se encuentran en riesgo de perderse. En el 2025, postularon 200 lugares, y resultaron elegidos 25, entre ellos el proyecto de los waru waru”, cuenta Juan Pablo de la Puente, director ejecutivo de World Monuments Fund Perú. El funcionario precisa que luego el proyecto, bajo el título de “Campos agrícolas waru waru de Acora”, tuvo que participar en otro concurso –Cultivating Resilience–, donde quedó seleccionado para obtener los fondos respectivos, junto con proyectos vinculados a las chinampas de Xochimilco, en México; el Central Park, de Nueva York; el huerto del rey, en el Palacio de Versalles; el foso de la Torre de Londres.
Con este apoyo y financiamiento, las cuatro comunidades, a través de la Asociación Aymara Suma Yapu, se pusieron manos a la obra. A partir de faenas comunales se organizaron para diseñar y construir los waru waru de la misma manera en que lo hacían sus abuelos: elevar la tierra del fondo de las lagunas para formar plataformas elevadas (camellones), fijar los taludes inclinados de soporte, y transformar el altiplano en geométricos campos de cultivo. Esta arquitectura agrícola, rodeada por canales de agua, contribuye a regular la temperatura del suelo, optimizando el uso del recurso hídrico, y reduciendo el impacto de inundaciones o sequías.
Papas con energía
El primer ciclo de siembra y cosecha desarrollado a partir del proyecto no solo ha sido exitoso –se han cosechado cerca de cuatro toneladas de papas nativas–, sino también ha llenado de orgullo a estas comunidades. “Nosotros como aimaras estamos orgullosos del legado que nos han dejado nuestros abuelos, ellos nos han heredado más de tres mil variedades de papas y cada una tiene un diferente atributo y gusto. Nosotros, como institución, buscamos recuperar esta forma de criar la chacra, con respeto a la madre tierra”, dice Eliana Apaza, directora ejecutiva de la Asociación Aymara Suma Yapu.
Ella define a los waru waru como una tecnología de punta ancestral frente a un cambio climático fuerte, y destaca su función termorreguladora en una región de temperaturas extremas. “Tienen un controlador –explica–, si hay poca lluvia se cierran las compuertas de los canales para que se mantenga la humedad del suelo, y si hay mucha lluvia se abren para que salga el agua. Asimismo, si hay heladas fuertes, el agua de los canales se calienta con los rayos del sol durante el día y en la noche irradia ese calor al suelo para que las plantitas no mueran. Además, en el agua, hay todo un ecosistema, vienen los patitos, vienen las aves migratorias, y eso hace que exista un abono natural, con lo cual se puede cultivar orgánicamente”.
Uno de los retos actuales es lograr la sostenibilidad y permanencia de esta técnica de cultivo. De la Puente destaca la organización de talleres para el registro de este conocimiento, el desarrollo de exposiciones, como la desarrollada en Proyectoamil, en Barranco, y la promoción de las comunidades y de sus productos en la actual feria Fusión por Gloria. “Sabemos que ese es un reto grande, pero el primer paso era generar estos encuentros en Lima, dar a conocer este valor ancestral y cultural, así como su utilidad práctica para enfrentar retos actuales. En ese camino, hemos hecho aliados importantes como el Centro Internacional de la Papa y Mater para estudiar las variedades de tubérculos producidos en los waru waru”, añade.
Además…
A saber
El domingo 6 de septiembre representantes de las comunidades de Acora ofrecerán sus productos en el mercado de la feria Fusión por Gloria, en la explanada Costa Verde, en Magdalena del Mar.

title: Fasting, prayer and a call for unity: Jewish community marks Yom Kippur in Casablanca
content: They turned out in large numbers on Monday, September 21, to observe the holiest day of the Jewish year. Addressing worshippers gathered in Casablanca, Serge Berdugo, secretary-general of the Council of Jewish Communities of Morocco, began by reflecting on the meaning of this day of fasting and prayer. “During this month of Elul [the sixth month of the Jewish civil calendar, Editor’s note], the gates of heaven are open to receive our prayers and supplications, so that the Eternal may forgive us all our sins,” he said.Yom Kippur, he recalled, is “one of the most solemn and sacred days in the Jewish calendar, when each person takes account of their actions and asks forgiveness from those they may have wronged.” Divine forgiveness, however, follows a particular order. Before turning to heaven, worshippers must first turn to one another. “Before asking for and receiving Hashem’s forgiveness, we must ask forgiveness from our fellow human beings for any wrong we may have done,” Berdugo stressed.The day brings a particularly significant period in the Hebrew calendar to a close. Yom Kippur is “the culmination of the period known as the ‘Days of Awe,’ which lead us towards repentance as we stand in judgment before God,” he explained.The door to forgiveness is open to all, on one condition. “All people have access to divine forgiveness if they acknowledge their faults and make amends for the injustices they have committed,” the community leader said, before returning to the central principle: “God can forgive sins committed against Him, but before that, we must obtain forgiveness for those we have committed against our fellow human beings.”Putting those words into practice, Berdugo himself asked for forgiveness. “For my part, I humbly ask forgiveness, Mehila, from all those whom I may inadvertently have offended,” he told the congregation.Berdugo said Yom Kippur also carries a message of hope. It is “a day of soul-searching, humility and repentance, when a person looks inward and deeply examines their actions,” but also “a day of love for those who hold on to the hope that people can live in peace and harmony,” he said. He extended that hope to the wider region. “We hope that the year now beginning will finally bring a peaceful and just resolution to the fratricidal conflicts that are bringing grief to the Middle East,” he said.This year’s observance took on added significance as it coincided with the 28th anniversary of the death of King Hassan II. Rabbi Hazout was invited to offer prayers for the repose of the late Sovereign’s soul, describing him as “forever present in our hearts.” He also prayed for the soul of “our revered Sultan, the late Mohammed V,” whom the community commended to God’s “holy mercy.”Casablanca’s Chief Rabbi Yossef Israël then offered solemn blessings for King Mohammed VI. Worshippers prayed that the Almighty would protect the Sovereign and grant him “health, joy and success in all his endeavors for the glory of eternal Morocco.”Prayers were also offered for the happiness, health and success of Crown Prince Moulay El Hassan, Princess Lalla Khadija, Prince Moulay Rachid and the entire Royal Family. “May God bless this honorable gathering and the Moroccan people,” Berdugo said, followed by an Amen from the congregation.Preserve, defend and pass onThe secretary-general of the Council of Jewish Communities of Morocco then addressed members of the Kahal, the congregation, directly with a message focused on the future. “At this time of profound change, it is the duty of each and every one of us to rally around the Community to safeguard and ensure the continuity of the tangible and intangible heritage of Moroccan Judaism,” he said. That effort, he added, requires “defending its ancestral values, preserving the achievements of our Community and ensuring its place within the social fabric of our country.”For Berdugo, history has already shown the way forward. “As recent history demonstrates, anything is possible if we return to the community spirit that prevailed for centuries,” he said. Two words, in his view, sum up that spirit: “unity and solidarity,” which he described as “the keys to the future of our community.”The address ended with wishes for the Jewish New Year. “May Hashem guide your steps. May this year 5787 bring health, joy and serenity to our homes, and peace to hearts and peoples throughout the world,” Berdugo said.The ceremony was attended by the wali, governors, city officials and rabbis, alongside members of Casablanca’s Jewish community.

title: Alice Kang’ethe: The economist fighting for a healthier Africa
content:
Early in Alice Kang'ethe's public-health career, on a trip to Mbita, a scorpion stung her. The pain was ferocious. She was far from a proper hospital, and her international health insurance was useless there. The immediate help at her disposal was a modest clinic, where health workers gave her an antidote and got her the care she needed.
"Those people saved my life," Alice says. It is, in a way, the whole argument she has built a career on: Fix the small clinic, and the rest of the country survives with it. Ignore it, and geography decides who lives.
Alice has spent 20 years chasing that idea across borders, first as a volunteer in Dar es Salaam. She had just returned from the London School of Economics (LSE), hoping to work in a think tank, using economics to influence policy.
"I came back to Kenya from LSE and reality hit. Unemployment. A friend asked if I would consider volunteering for a foundation just starting out in HIV care and treatment. My parents were frustrated," she says.
She now runs the Beginnings Fund, built with a coalition that includes the Gates Foundation and the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, to attack what she calls the "core drivers of death" in maternal and newborn health. It has raised $493 million (Sh63 billion) and pushed $199 million Sh25 billion) into 30 grants across six African countries.
"I could do something here that will touch millions of lives on my continent."
TIME magazine put her on its inaugural TIME100 Philanthropy list this year. Her mother called it, simply, the fulfilment of her dream, the same mother who told a young girl decades ago that she would have to work twice as hard to be taken half as seriously.
What frustrates her now is the pace of change. “My struggle is, it’s not moving fast enough.”
You've had such a good run, haven't you?
I would say so. I'm not done yet. But I'm proud of what we have achieved. I say "we" because I've had a team.
Do you remember how you stood out, as a young woman getting into this career?
I'm actually an economist by training. After high school I went to Catholic University of Eastern Africa and majored in Economics, then to the London School of Economics (LSE). My dream was to be in a think tank, using economics to influence policy. Somehow I ended up in public health instead, I'd say by accident.
I came back to Kenya from LSE and reality hit. Unemployment. A friend asked if I would consider volunteering for a foundation just starting out in HIV care and treatment as I waited for a full-time job. My parents were frustrated, they had funded my postgraduate studies in London, no small feat, and now I needed money to go and volunteer. Reluctantly, they supported me.
My first stop was Dar es Salaam, thrown straight into the deep end. The more senior volunteers had to fly back to the US, and left me
to convene stakeholders from across Tanzania, government, development agencies, experts, to develop the country's first national HIV care and treatment plan. I had no office, I was working out of a hotel room, and most people were essentially asking, 'who are you, what mandate do you even have?' I did not give up.
Every time I go back today and see people sitting calmly in those clinics, no stigma, getting their treatment, it is so fulfilling.
From there I went to South Africa, a different scale altogether, a government not yet convinced it should support care at scale. Our first attempt failed. I left, joined KPMG for a year, and no sooner had I settled in than my former team lead called to say they were setting up an office in Kenya. I went right back.
Why did you go back, and why economics in the first place?
Because I cherished the experience. The people, the patients, the doctors, former President Bill Clinton himself. But also I realised I could do something that would impact millions of people.
I hear doctors who've moved from clinical practice to public health use this analogy: I could see one patient at a time in my clinic, or influence millions at a time. I got drawn into that. At the Clinton Foundation it was, here's a problem, go solve it, how you get there is up to you. I enjoyed that.
And economics, because I have a problem with the way Africa is described. I strongly believe there's a place for economic policy to lift people out of poverty.
What's been the most difficult thing you've ever had to do?
As a volunteer in South Africa, convincing the government that it was a moral imperative to provide care and treatment to everyone infected with HIV. Getting people with decision-making power to do the right thing, when you think it's obvious, but it isn't.
I see the same today in maternal and newborn health. No woman should die from preventable causes bringing life into the world, but we've almost normalised these deaths.
On a more practical level, fundraising. The world has waves and fads. There's a time HIV was very well funded. We see that too in maternal and child health, these peaks and troughs, when it needs to stay on the priority list for the long haul.
Go back to childhood a little. What do you remember, and what did you want then?
I was born in Nairobi, then my parents moved to Tigoni. My father was a banker with Barclays. Later we moved to Nakuru, to a farm. It was difficult for me because I'd lived in the city. I used to admire air hostesses, wanted to be one, but my father shut that down immediately, said that was no career.
Growing up, what I remember most is struggling with inequities. My parents weren't rich, but we didn't lack, we went to public schools, we had meals, the basics. In high school it was in the dormitory, seeing a girl with nothing in her box.
I still remember, from a very young age, struggling with why some children didn't have shoes, why they looked so ragged.
I believe everything I've done since has been toward social justice. I still struggle with it today. You go to some hospitals, find four premature babies sharing one incubator and ask, are these children of a lesser God?
In this season, are there habits you're trying to unlearn?
I'm trying to stop and smell the roses more. In academics, in my career, I invested everything into the work. Some of my friends say I take life too seriously, that I should stop, celebrate what I've done. So I'm doing more of that now.
You've a stellar career. What's one thing you failed at, and what did it teach you?
At the Clinton Health Access Initiative, I was given a programme on prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV. We succeeded in preventing transmission at delivery. But mothers still needed to breastfeed, and still carried the virus, and the science for that wasn't advanced yet. So, in essence, we failed.
Babies born HIV-negative eventually turned positive through breastfeeding. There was the option of infant formula, but that brought complications around clean water, and you could save a child from HIV only to lose them to dehydration and diarrhoea.
That taught me that much as we were the crazy ones who thought we could change the world, and for the most part we did, we needed to bring everyone along. We jumped ahead of the science, assuming the rest would catch up. Ambition must be matched with reality.
Is there anything you've always wanted to do but haven't gotten around to?
I keep saying I want to retire in Nanyuki, on a farm. I think I'm a rural girl now. I haven't gotten around to finding that place, that solace, and I realise I don't have so much time left, so I'd better do it. I think of retirement more now, in part because I believe in empowering others to carry the baton. I don't want to hold it for too long before I hand over.
Are there things you struggle with as a female leader that male leaders of your cadre don't?
Certainly, we haven't moved past that. Early in my career, we were supporting the Kenyan government to hire additional nurses and doctors, the money had been put in Treasury but staff hadn't been paid.
I kept urging the leads to honour that commitment, and one of them told me, 'young girl, don't get emotional, it's normal for doctors and nurses to wait six months for their first salary.' I said, but the money is already there, we're failing them by not moving it.
I don't think if the person raising that concern had been a man, the response would have been the same. As women, especially African women, you have to work twice as hard to earn that level of respect. I've sat in a waiting room while someone said, 'we're still waiting for your boss', only for my colleague to correct them, 'this is the boss.'
What personal fears keep you up at night?
I'm a mum to a 10-year-old girl, and I think about what happens if I'm not there, who takes care of her. And whether she'll turn out well, whether I'm teaching her the real strokes of life, or sheltering her too much.
Where do you get your affirmation from now?
My family, especially my husband. Even on tough days he's good at telling me I'm doing a great job. And my mother, a core pillar of my strength. In May, when I got the TIME100 Philanthropy recognition, she told me I had fulfilled her dream. She's one of my biggest cheerleaders.
What's your struggle in this season of your life?
Speed. The rate at which I want to see change. I feel it every time I sit in rooms where Africa is described negatively, especially on maternal and newborn mortality. I know the approach of working with governments is the right one, but I want to inject more pace into it.
What's your love language?
Service. I do gifting too, but acts of service is the predominant one. I believe in showing up.
Is there anything you'd like to share that you thought I'd ask?
Early in my career, leading the Kenya programme, I was on a trip to Beta Point, today's Homa Bay County, when I felt something creep up my trousers. I'd been stung by a scorpion.
What stuck with me is that health workers at the local health centre treated me quickly, crushed the scorpion, gave me the antidote. My international health insurance didn't matter in that moment. Those were the people who saved my life.
I tell that story because it's why I'm such a strong believer in building systems for everyone. That experience grounded me, and it's part of why I keep chasing equity for all.
If the Level Five hospital is functioning, it's for all of us. Getting anywhere else for treatment at the time was far-fetched. That grounded me, and it's part of why I keep chasing equity for all.
If you were reincarnated, what profession would you choose? And what do you do now to unwind?
I think I'd get into large-scale farming, combining another inequity I care about, food security, with the peace and serene life I look forward to in retirement. To unwind I love to travel to peaceful, serene places. Water calms me a lot. I also read, and I take time with friends, and with my daughter.

title: Alberto de la Rosa, una vida de orgullo por la música jarocha
content:
El arpista es considerado uno de los mayores exponentes del instrumento en el mundo // Es fundador del grupo Tlen Huicani, que hoy cumple 53 años
Sábado 12 de septiembre de 2026, p. 3
“El movimiento arpista de Veracruz está vivo y con mucha fuerza”, afirma Alberto de la Rosa, compositor, arreglista y uno de los mayores exponentes del arpa jarocha en el mundo. Para el artista de 79 años, si antes ese instrumento estaba en Mandinga y Boca del Río, ahora Xalapa es uno de los principales centros de esta expresión, junto con Coatepec y Xico.
En el contexto del 53 aniversario del grupo Tlen Huicani, que se cumple hoy, De la Rosa afirma a La Jornada que la vigencia del arpa jarocha se explica por el apoyo de la Universidad Veracruzana (UV), los ayuntamientos locales, y sobre todo por el interés de la población en estudiar y ejecutar este instrumento.
Como muestra de su vitalidad, citó El Jarochódromo y el récord La Bamba, encuentros que reúnen a cientos de personas que bailan son jarocho en Coatepec y Xalapa, y que este año tendrán su octava y duodécima edición, respectivamente. También mencionó el Festival Internacional del Arpa Alberto de la Rosa, que en junio se realizó por cuarto año consecutivo, y convoca a músicos nacionales y extranjeros.
Entre los exponentes actuales, De la Rosa destaca a músicos jóvenes, como Horacio Martínez y Raúl Monge, quien canta, toca arpa y tiene en su haber más de 50 composiciones. Resalta la presencia de las mujeres, que en los años recientes se han interesado en la ejecución del instrumento.
Sobresale el caso de su hija María Cristina, quien en abril ganó el Premio del Público en el Concurso Mundial de Arpa 2026, que se celebra cada dos años en Holanda. “Logró ese reconocimiento por la emoción que despiertan sus interpretaciones y consiguió que los ojos del mundo artístico se fijen en México”.
De la Rosa se acercó a la música y aprendió a tocar la guitarra en Acayucan, en el sur de Veracruz, donde vivió hasta los 12 años. Recuerda que en un tiempo en que la radio y la televisión no eran frecuentes en los hogares veracruzanos, las familias se organizaban para realizar tertulias.
Los domingos, su mamá ponía una tarima y la música del arpista Andrés Huesca para bailar en su casa. “Era algo familiar; incluso, la palabra fandango ni siquiera se usaba, nada más decían: ‘va haber tarima’”, menciona.
“¿Yo por qué voy a tocar a Elvis?”
Entre los años 1950 y 1960, cuando el rock irrumpió con fuerza en México, De la Rosa quedó cautivado con Elvis Presley, y si bien lo siguió por un rato, llegó un momento en que se cuestionó sus gustos: “¿Yo por qué voy a tocar esa música, si soy veracruzano y mi música es el son jarocho?”.
A los 12 años, durante una semana del estudiante de la Escuela Preparatoria de Xalapa, presenció un concierto de arpa que desencadenó su interés por el instrumento. “Estaba escuchando al intérprete, cuando un amigo me contó que en su casa había un arpa, le pregunté quién la tocaba y me respondió que nadie. Así que le pedí que me la prestara y al otro día fui por ella”.
De la Rosa aprendió a tocar el arpa de forma autodidacta: escuchando discos y acercándose a quienes tocaban. “Los músicos de aquel tiempo eran celosos, quienes aprendían a tocar lo hacían de su papá o del tío. Yo me arrimaba a ellos y poco a poco hice amistad con algunos, hasta que Arcadio Solís me invitó a tocar con él”.
En las épocas de Carnaval o de Semana Santa, De la Rosa se unía a varios conjuntos. “Para que me dejaran andar con ellos no aceptaba nada de lo que ellos ganaban. Y como iba aprendiendo, y se corrió la voz de que no cobraba, otros grupos me empezaron a llamar”.
Después de un breve paso por la Escuela Nacional de Música, en la Ciudad de México, que se vio interrumpido por el movimiento estudiantil de 1968, De la Rosa regresó a Xalapa, adonde ingresó a la Normal Veracruzana Enrique C. Rébsamen, que tenía una intensa actividad artística. Era la época de Miguel Vélez en la danza, Mateo Oliva en la música y Antolín Guzmán, músico muy interesado en los jóvenes.
Como parte del Ballet Folklórico Veracruz, De la Rosa hizo una gira por Sudamérica, que se convirtió en una epifanía. “Me encontré con la sorpresa de que en todos los países había arpa; establecí relación con los intérpretes, traje un paquete de música e incluso un arpa de Venezuela, que es diferente a la nuestra”.
Después de aquellos recorridos, conformó el grupo Tlen Huicani, que dio su primer concierto oficial el 12 de septiembre de 1973, en el Teatro del Estado Ignacio de la Llave. Pronto, la UV se incorporó a la agrupación junto con la Orquesta Sinfónica de Xalapa y Orbis Tertius. “Más que pagar un sueldo, con la bandera de la universidad comenzamos a recibir invitaciones de muchas partes del mundo”.
Con casi 53 años de trayectoria, Tlen Huicani ha tenido presencia en 62 países. “Hemos dado la vuelta al mundo saliendo por el este y regresando por el oeste... infinidad de grabaciones, y Xalapa se ha convertido en la Ciudad del arpa”, subrayó.
Cuando se le pregunta qué enseñanza le ha dejado este instrumento, De la Rosa responde: el orgullo por la música veracruzana. “Ahora que hay una invasión de música de todo tipo, de alguna que podemos decir corriente, donde el éxito es la vulgaridad de los textos, tocar música jarocha es ir en contra de todo eso”.
En un mensaje para las nuevas generaciones, el arpista les pide “que echen un ojo y pongan el oído a la música folklórica. Muchos la consideran de segunda, pero no es así, a diferencia de otras expresiones que son pasajeras, ésta es nuestro orgullo y se mantiene en el tiempo”.
A las autoridades pide que abran más foros que permitan el intercambio de grupos como Tlen Huicani, con exponentes como Fernando de la Mora o la cantante Olivia Gorra, con quienes han alternado en otras ocasiones.
De cara al futuro, habló de la necesidad de documentar a los exponentes del arpa veracruzana y sus composiciones. “Hay gente que me ha preguntado: ‘¿cómo quisieras ser recordado?’ No, no me interesa ser recordado así. A mí me gustaría que sea recordado todo aquello por lo que he luchado, que sea recordado el son jarocho y que se fortalezca. Yo sólo fui y he sido uno de tantos que va pasando”, concluyó Alberto de la Rosa.

title: Sao Tomé: Open-air Tchiloli theatre continues to thrive
content:
São Tomé and Príncipe
Sporting a range of outfits accessorised with beards, wigs and hats, actors on Sao Tomé perform a medieval European tragedy on the island off Africa's west coast. Brought to the archipelago nation more than 500 years ago by Portuguese colonialists, the tradition of open-air Tchiloli theatre continues to prove popular with residents and tourists to this day.
One of the troop's members believes its popularity comes from its championing of justice.
Marc Carvalho has been in the troop for 35 years, and says, "people love this culture because it speaks about something very real: justice. Justice does not distinguish between rich and poor. Whether one is poor or rich, man or woman, there must be justice. That’s exactly it."
The play's script is in Old Portuguese; it draws from the legends linked to the Carolingian dynasty, which ruled over the majority of western Europe from the eighth to the 10th centuries AD.
Spectators say the themes continue to resonate, which is what has preserved the tradition for so long.
"It conveys a very important message. Basically, it says that justice is something that, how shall I put it, concerns both the poor and the rich. No matter the religion, no matter the social class. In other words, wealth, that sort of thing. Everything has to be fair. Whoever sows evil reaps evil," says Maribel Borja.
It's intense work, with the troop spending several hours performing at a time. But member Jardel Moniz Fernandez says he finds it energising and hopes to one day include his children in the group.
"I have two children, and soon I’ll start teaching my oldest to play the character of Kata, a young boy who, in the play, has to deliver a letter. I’ll start getting him ready now so that he can also be part of the group," he says.
Open-air Tchiloli theatre is now a UNESCO-listed tradition

title: En el Ateneo Luis Mariano Rivera de Carúpano rindieron honor a la Virgen del Valle
content:
El Ateneo Luis Mariano Rivera de Carúpano, municipio Bermúdez del estado Sucre, rindió homenaje a la Patrona de Oriente, la Virgen del Valle, con una velada cultural que incluyó la celebración de una Rucaristía, que presidió el presbítero Jesús Villarroel, párroco de la catedral; además de una exposición de imágenes de "Vallita" hechas por artistas locales; así como una muestra de danza, cantos y para cerrar un galerón.
Auristela Tenías, comisionada de Turismo y Cultura de la institución dijo que pidieron a la Virgen que sea inspiración para un Carúpano más humano y cristiano.
La velada contó con la participación de los grupos de danza Expresión Dramática Octágono, Fundación Niño Jesús, la Escuela de Ballet y Danza Domingo Renault y la escuela de ballet y danza Lucy Cordero de la Casa de la Cultura de Playa Grande.
Resaltó la realización del galerón infantil con la Fundación Cultural Guaraúnos, con cinco niños que cantaron décimas a la Santa Virgen. También contaron con la participación del grupo de cuerdas del ateneo, el cantante Elías Rodríguez y la cultora Catalina Núñez.
Recordar
Por su parte, el padre Jesús Villarroel señaló que a la Virgen del Valle no se le celebra solo un día, sino que es una devoción constante para los orientales.
“Este día nos expresa que la Virgen del Valle no es un día, es todos los días. Para los orientales esta celebración se prolonga, por eso hoy seguimos celebrando la fiesta de nuestra madre”.
Villarroel recordó a los fallecidos por los terremotos y pidió orar por ellos, “Pedimos por tantos hermanos venezolanos fallecidos y también recordando todo este acontecimiento que vivió nuestro país”, señaló.
Sucre / Yumelys Díaz

title: Senado aprova garantia do direito à natureza para crianças e adolescentes
content:
Senado aprova garantia do direito à natureza para crianças e adolescentes
Chamado de ECA Ambiental, proposta define como dever da família, da sociedade e do Estado a efetivação do contato com o meio natural
Chamado de ECA Ambiental, proposta define como dever da família, da sociedade e do Estado a efetivação do contato com o meio natural
Um projeto que estabelece princípios e diretrizes para garantir o direito da criança e do adolescente à natureza, “com absoluta prioridade”, foi aprovado no Senado na última quarta-feira (2). O PL 2.225/2024 da deputada federal Laura Carneiro (PSD-RJ) agora segue para sanção presidencial.
A proposta estabelece prioridade no recebimento de amparo em situações de riscos socioambientais e climáticos, além de assegurar “o acesso a áreas naturais saudáveis”, o “brincar livre” e a “educação baseada na natureza”. Terão prioridade na efetivação dessas garantias às crianças na primeira infância e aquelas com deficiência. De acordo com o texto, o atendimento pleno desse direito é objetivo a ser buscado pela União, estados, Distrito Federal e municípios.
Para consolidar essas diretrizes, o texto inclui o direito da infância ao meio ambiente equilibrado entre os princípios da Política Nacional do Meio Ambiente (Lei 6.938, de 1981). Além disso, o Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA – Lei 8.069, de 1990) passa a definir como dever da família, da sociedade e do Estado a efetivação do contato com o meio natural. Por fim, a Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima (Lei 12.187, de 2009) ganha um dispositivo que torna obrigatória a atuação governamental prioritária na mitigação dos impactos climáticos sobre esse público.
Em sua justificativa, o senador Alessandro Vieira, relator do projeto, destaca as soluções baseadas na natureza esperadas. “Pátios naturalizados, arborização, sombreamento, permeabilidade do solo, manejo integrado das águas, uso de espécies nativas e integração com o território são medidas compatíveis com soluções baseadas na natureza e com políticas contemporâneas de resiliência urbana”, afirma.
A aprovação é resultado de uma construção conjunta entre parlamentares, organizações da sociedade civil, especialistas em crianças e adolescentes, que participaram da mobilização em torno da proposta desde o início de sua tramitação.
Para o Alana, organização em prol das crianças, a aprovação é um avanço importante para incorporar a proteção de crianças e adolescentes às políticas de prevenção, adaptação e resposta à crise climática no Brasil.
“O avanço do ECA Ambiental reforça a necessidade de colocar a infância no centro das decisões sobre o clima e abre caminho para que as políticas de adaptação climática passem a considerar, de forma mais concreta, as necessidades de crianças e adolescentes. É também um passo para preparar melhor escolas, cidades e territórios para uma realidade em que eventos extremos tendem a ser cada vez mais presentes”, diz Tayanne Galeno, coordenadora de Relações Governamentais do Alana.
A aprovação do ECA Ambiental ganha peso ainda maior diante das projeções para o super El Niño de 2026/2027. Os cenários climáticos alertam para chuvas acima da média no Sul durante o último trimestre de 2026, períodos de menor precipitação na Amazônia e em parte do Nordeste, além de temperaturas mais altas em grande parte do país. A combinação desses fatores pode aumentar o risco de incêndios florestais e a ocorrência de eventos extremos, com impactos especialmente graves para crianças e adolescentes.
“O trabalho, porém, não termina com a aprovação da lei: será preciso transformar o avanço no Congresso em políticas públicas capazes de responder aos impactos que crianças e adolescentes já enfrentam e aos que podem surgir nos próximos anos”, conclui Tayanne.

title: When the Land Speaks, the Community Listens: How Indigenous Self-governance Protects Climate Knowledge and Food Systems in Abim, Karamoja, Uganda
content: When the Land Speaks, the Community Listens: How Indigenous Self-governance Protects Climate Knowledge and Food Systems in Abim, Karamoja, Uganda tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 14:27 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe For generations, Indigenous communities in Abim District, Karamoja, in northeastern Uganda, have depended on a deep relationship with their land, water, animals, forests, and natural environment. This relationship has guided how communities make decisions, resolve challenges, protect resources, and prepare for uncertain times. Long before climate change became a global concern, communities had their own ways of understanding environmental changes. Cattle and goats became unusually restless or vocal, signaling upcoming heavy winds or rainfall. Elders observed birds’ behavior and the flowering of trees. They used the alignment and brightness of specific stars and the moon to gauge seasonal timing and predict long dry cycles. Haruspicy (reading goat intestines) was used to forecast weather patterns, seasonal rainfall quality, and impending environmental or social shocks. These observations helped communities decide when to plant crops, how to prepare for drought, and how to protect needed resources. This knowledge was not written but was carried through stories, community gatherings, cultural practices, family teachings, and intergenerational relationships. In Abim, governance has never been only about leaders and decision-making structures but foremost about responsibility to the community, the land, and future generations. Today, this relationship faces increasing pressure. Climate change has brought longer drought periods and unpredictable rainfall, leading to declining pastures and crop failures and increasing challenges to food security, famine, and death. Many Indigenous practices and knowledge systems are at risk of disappearing as younger generations have fewer opportunities to learn from Elders. Indigenous self-governance in Abim is built on collective responsibility. Important decisions affecting land, natural resources, community well being, and social relationships have traditionally been discussed through community consultation involving Elders, women, clan representatives, and other members. Leadership is understood not simply as authority over others, but as a responsibility to serve and protect community interests. Elders play an important role as custodians of history, cultural values, and environmental knowledge, carrying memories of droughts, food shortages, traditional farming practices, and emergency management. When disagreements arise, Indigenous approaches focus on dialogue, mediation, and restoring relationships. The purpose is not only to determine who is right or wrong, but to rebuild trust because community survival depends on cooperation. A reflection shared during community knowledge discussions highlights this understanding: “Our Elders taught us that the land is not something we own alone. We are only caretakers for those who will come after us. When we sit together and listen to each other, we find solutions that protect both people and nature. The knowledge of our ancestors helped our communities survive difficult seasons. Protecting this knowledge means protecting who we are.” Women as Keepers of Knowledge In Abim, women have always played a central role in sustaining communities, carrying essential knowledge of seeds, traditional crops, food preservation, medicinal plants, and wild foods that provide nutrition during difficult periods and support family and community survival. As custodians of this knowledge, women have relied on passed-down teachings about which foods can support families and which Indigenous crops can withstand harsh environmental conditions. Traditional crops such as millet, sorghum, and other Indigenous varieties have provided resilience because they are adapted to local conditions and have survived through generations of careful selection. These knowledge systems face increasing challenges. Changing lifestyles, climate pressures, and reduced opportunities for intergenerational learning are contributing to the loss of Indigenous practices. Strengthening women’s participation in community decision-making helps ensure that climate adaptation strategies include the experiences of those who have long protected household food systems. A reflection from women leaders during community dialogues expressed this connection: “Women have always carried important knowledge in our homes and communities. We know the seeds that survive, the foods that help families during difficult times, and the ways our mothers protected the environment. When women participate in decisions about land and resources, the whole community benefits because our experiences are included.” Restoring the Relationship with Nature One of the greatest strengths of Indigenous communities is the ability to understand environmental changes through generations of observation. Elders have traditionally used signs from nature as early warning systems. Changes in plants, animals, insects, and weather patterns provided important information about potential droughts, changes in rainfall, or challenges affecting crops and livestock. The flowering of certain trees, changes in bird behavior, the appearance of insects, and the availability of specific wild foods were carefully observed and discussed within communities. This knowledge, based on experience, careful observation, and adaptation, represents generations of relationships with the environment. As climate change grows more unpredictable and Elders become fewer in number, there is a growing need to document and strengthen these knowledge systems. Food security in Abim has always depended on Indigenous Knowledge of crops that can withstand challenging environmental conditions. For generations, communities have preserved crop varieties that withstand drought, require fewer external inputs, and provide important food sources during difficult seasons. Many Indigenous seeds are becoming less common due to changing agricultural practices and reduced transmission of Traditional Knowledge. Community efforts to preserve Indigenous seeds are helping restore local food systems. Women, Elders, and young people are working together to document traditional crops, share planting knowledge, and encourage the continued use of climate-resilient varieties. Protecting Indigenous seeds is more than protecting agriculture. It is protecting identity, independence, and the ability of future generations to sustain themselves. Indigenous Governance as a Pathway Forward Indigenous governance also guides how communities relate to natural resources. Land is not viewed only as an economic resource. It is connected to culture, history, spirituality, and community identity. Community members have recognized their responsibilities to protect important trees, water sources, grazing areas, and culturally significant places. Through collective action, communities are strengthening environmental protection practices, including restoring degraded areas, protecting water sources, and responsibly managing communal resources. These actions are based on the understanding that humans are part of nature and have responsibilities to maintain ecological balance. The survival of Indigenous governance depends on whether knowledge can continue moving from one generation to another. Young people in Abim are becoming increasingly involved in learning from Elders, participating in environmental activities, and understanding their responsibilities as community members. Intergenerational learning creates a connection between the wisdom of Elders and the energy and creativity of young people. Youth who understand the importance of Indigenous knowledge can become future custodians of culture, land, and community resilience. Indigenous self-governance remains highly relevant in today’s world. As communities globally face climate change, environmental degradation, and social challenges, Indigenous governance systems offer important lessons. Communities create stronger solutions when they participate in decisions affecting their lives. Environmental protection becomes stronger when people maintain relationships with the land. Women’s knowledge and leadership are essential for resilience. Elders carry valuable knowledge that complements modern approaches. Culture and identity are sources of strength during times of uncertainty. In Abim, Indigenous self-governance continues to guide communities in understanding their environment, protecting resources, strengthening food systems, and preparing for the future. The knowledge held by Elders, women, and community leaders is not simply cultural heritage, but a living resource that contributes to climate resilience, food security, and community well being. As the world searches for solutions to environmental challenges, Indigenous communities remind us of the importance of listening to the land, Elders, and communities that have cared for their environments for generations. Oscar Ogole (Karamojong) is Executive Director of Community Development Shield Uganda. Main photo: Bridging generations in Karamoja. title: Tuku whenua: A day Aucklanders can come to know and share
content: As we celebrate Te Wiki o te Reo Māori, it feels right to remember an important moment for Ngāti Whātua and Auckland. These kaupapa meet this week. Both ask us to listen, learn and reconnect with the people, places and stories of Tāmaki Makaurau. I grew up in Auckland knowing I was Ngāti Whātua, but not all the kōrero about the whenua beneath my feet. I knew the streets, beaches and landmarks, but few of their original names or histories. I knew the city I could see, but not the story underneath it. The history was close. My father, Hapi Pihema, was one of many kaumātua and cultural leaders who worked to strengthen our people and rebuild our cultural estate. He helped protect and pass on the kōrero. As a boy, I did not understand that work. Sometimes the stories closest to us take the longest to hear. As I grew older, I learned more about Apihai Te Kawau and the tūpuna beside him. In 1840, Te Kawau sent people north to invite governor William Hobson to Tāmaki Makaurau. He saw that a new township could bring peace, trade, opportunity, and hoped Māori and Pākehā could build a relationship together. On 18 September 1840, Te Kawau and his people made 3,000 acres available to establish Auckland. This is often called a gift, but tuku whenua means much more. The land was not handed over and forgotten. It was an act of mana, leadership and manaakitanga, offered in the hope that people would care for one another and build a future together. Sadly, that is not how the story unfolded. Ngāti Whātua lost almost all its land. By the 1950s, our people at Ōkahu Bay were virtually landless, and homes were pulled down before a royal visit. Years later, Takaparawhau became an important fight for justice and the survival of our people. Joe Pihema (Photo: supplied, additional design: Tina Tiller) That hurt is part of the story, but not all of it. We also remember the courage and generosity of Te Kawau and our tūpuna. They looked ahead with hope. We must hold both sides: the future they offered and what happened when the promise was not kept. For me, learning this history has been about finding my place. It explains why some places carry so much feeling, why Māori names matter and why whenua can feel familiar even when its stories are unknown. It has shown me what I must pass on. Today, Ngāti Whātua will gather at Auckland’s viaduct to remember Te Kawau and his people. Through karanga, karakia, whaikōrero and mōteatea, we will honour 1840. Beside the Waitematā, we remember the hopes our tūpuna held for the city that would grow here. This remembrance is not only for Ngāti Whātua. It is an open invitation to Auckland. That spirit sits at the heart of the Poumatua Festival, finishing Saturday 19 September. For the first time on this scale, Te Kawau, tuku whenua and Auckland’s beginnings are being shared openly. Through kōrero, kapa haka, learning, creativity and whakawhanaungatanga, we welcome Aucklanders from every background. We invite people to get out and explore this whenua. Walk across the land. Learn the Māori names. Find out about the maunga, waterways, bays and old pathways beneath our roads. Reach into those connections. They help us understand where we live and build identity and belonging. Whether your family has been here for generations or recently arrived, there is a place for you in this story of our shared city. Then, in 1951-2, the residents of the papakāinga (village) were forcibly evicted, and Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei’s last settlement was burned down to ‘tidy’ the area for the visit of Queen Elizabeth II. (Photo: Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei) Perhaps 18 September can become a day Aucklanders come to know and share for themselves. A day to stop, look around and think about what made this city possible. If people pick it up in their own way, its meaning will grow. In time, Auckland may choose to recognise it officially as a day of importance. My hope is simple: I want our children to know that Tāmaki Makaurau has a story shaped by courage, generosity and hope. On 18 September, Ngāti Whātua invites Aucklanders to remember with us and reconnect with that beginning. It can be a day we share as proud Aucklanders, each of us searching for connection and identity. By knowing this story, we may come to know our city, and one another, a little better. More Reading

title: A Little-Known Fact: Pakuri’s Lands Stretch Across Two Regions
content:
A little-known fact about Pakuri, better known as St Cuthbert’s Mission, is that the country’s only titled Indigenous community in Region Four actually stretches across two administrative regions.
The Amerindian Peoples Association (APA), in an update on its ongoing community outreach, said part of Pakuri’s titled lands lies in Region Five, even though the community itself is recognised as the only Indigenous village in Region Four.
Located along the Mahaica River, Pakuri is primarily home to the Lokono people and is one of Guyana’s best-known Indigenous communities. Its relative proximity to Georgetown has also made it an important centre for Indigenous culture and heritage.
The APA said Pakuri’s circumstances are notably different from those of many hinterland communities.
“Unlike several of the hinterland regions, where numerous Indigenous villages are spread across large territories, Pakuri is recognised as the only Indigenous village in the Demerara-Mahaica Region.”
But the community’s administrative geography is more complicated than its designation as a Region Four village might suggest.
“But many of you may not know that the village straddles two regions! Part of Pakuri’s lands falls within Administrative Region Five (Mahaica-Berbice). So if you didn’t know, now you know!”
The revelation highlights an important distinction between administrative boundaries and Indigenous land ownership in Guyana. While the country is divided into ten administrative regions for purposes of governance and public administration, Indigenous communities may hold titled lands extending across those regional boundaries.
Pakuri’s location and history have given it particular cultural significance. The community, historically known as St Cuthbert’s Mission, is associated with the Lokono nation and is frequently identified as a cultural centre because of its accessibility from the coast and Georgetown.
The APA’s latest update came as its outreach team moved from Region Three into Region Four after spending longer than initially planned in Region Three.
With characteristic humour, the organisation acknowledged the extended stay.
“We know we said we were overnighting in Region Three, but spent more than one night there. So, we will just pretend that it was just one long night.”
The APA then announced its move into Region Four and drew attention to Pakuri as a significant Indigenous community in the region.
“Today, we are moving on to Region Four, and we are sure many of us also know of the only titled Indigenous Community in the Region, Pakuri or commonly known as St Cuthbert’s Mission.”
The community’s lands crossing into Region Five means that, despite Pakuri’s recognition as Region Four’s only Indigenous village, its territorial footprint does not fit neatly within a single administrative boundary.
The detail is more than a geographical curiosity. It is a reminder that the history, land rights and territorial realities of Guyana’s Indigenous communities can extend beyond the administrative lines used to divide the country.

title: THÉÂTRE - Tropy Ilo croise amour et rancœur dans Voamaintilany
content: Le Tropy Ilo présente ce dimanche, à l’Ivokolo Analakely, « Voamaintilany », une pièce de théâtre malgache qui mêle amour, trahison et vengeance.Les membres de la Tropy Ilo réunis autour de « Voamaintilany ».Certaines blessures du passé peuvent se transmettre d’une génération à l’autre. C’est autour de cette idée que le Tropy Ilo présente « Voamaintilany », une pièce écrite par Nivo Hary, ce dimanche à l’Ivokolo Analakely.L’histoire met en scène trois amis dont la relation bascule après une trahison, un détournement d’argent et des manœuvres dirigées contre l’un d’eux. Des années plus tard, la victime revient animée par un désir de vengeance. Entre-temps, leurs enfants, qui ignorent les conflits du passé, tombent amoureux. « Le passé peut avoir des conséquences sur la vie et l’avenir des enfants », souligne un membre de la troupe.Le titre de la pièce fait référence à une plante aux couleurs rouge et noire, qui symbolise les contrastes de l’existence, entre joie et tristesse, espoir et déception. La représentation débutera à 14h 30, après l’ouverture des portes à 13h 30. Elle durera environ une heure et demie, sans entracte, et sera divisée en trois parties. Des chansons malgaches spécialement composées pour la pièce accompagneront l’histoire jusqu’au morceau final, « Voamaintilany ».Dix-huit ans de théâtre malgacheLa troupe a également porté une attention particulière aux aspects techniques du spectacle, notamment à l’audibilité des comédiens, à la sonorisation et aux éclairages.Le Tropy Ilo célèbre cette année ses 18 ans d’existence. La troupe a intégré officiellement la FMTM (Fikambanan’ny Mpanao Teatra Malagasy) en 2007. Elle œuvre à la revalorisation de la culture et du théâtre malgaches à travers des créations mêlant satire politique, humour et drame social. Ses représentations cherchent notamment à sensibiliser le public, à transmettre des leçons de vie et à contribuer à l’éducation des jeunes générations dans le respect des « fomba malagasy ».La mise en scène de « Voamaintilany » est assurée par Haja Ravaloson, actif depuis plusieurs années dans le théâtre et formateur de plusieurs troupes. La pièce a été préparée pendant près de 1 an, avec un travail consacré aux dialogues, aux mouvements, aux chants et aux aspects techniques du spectacle.Cassie Ramiandrasoa

title: At 4, he lost his NYPD father on 9/11; 25 years later, he wears his badge
content:
At four years of age, Casey Kloepfer was too young to understand why his father never came home from work. Twenty-five years later, he carries that loss into the same department his father served, wearing his father's badge number and playing for the NYPD lacrosse team his father helped create, states an online report by NYC Government website. For Casey, the connection to his father is not confined to a photograph, a memorial or a family story. It is woven into the uniform he wears and the department he chose to join.
A father lost on September 11
Ronnie Kloepfer was an NYPD officer who was killed in the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. He was among the thousands of first responders who rushed toward danger as others tried to escape. His death left behind a family that, like so many others, had to navigate life without someone who had been at its center. Ronnie's connection to the NYPD extended beyond his work as a police officer. He was also instrumental in establishing the department's lacrosse team, bringing together officers through a sport he loved and the team would eventually become an unexpected bridge between generations.
Following his father's path
A quarter-century after September 11, Casey became an NYPD officer himself. His decision gave a new meaning to a legacy that could easily have remained rooted in the past.
He now wears his father's badge number, carrying a small but deeply personal reminder of the man whose career ended before Casey was old enough to understand it.
Casey is also part of the same lacrosse tradition his father helped establish. Alongside other officers whose families share similar connections to the department, he keeps alive something that began long before the attacks. The significance is particularly powerful because the NYPD's relationship with September 11 did not end when the World Trade Center towers fell. Hundreds of officers who responded that day and worked at Ground Zero in the months that followed have since died from illnesses linked to their service.
A legacy that keeps moving forward
The story of Casey and his father reflects a larger reality within the NYPD. The department has spent 25 years carrying the memory of those it lost while welcoming new generations who were children, or not yet born, when the attacks happened. For younger officers, September 11 can feel like distant history. For families such as the Kloepfers, it remains personal. Casey's uniform, badge number and place on his father's lacrosse team bring those two eras together. Ronnie's life was cut short on September 11, but the things he built did not disappear with him. His son now serves in the department he once served, and the lacrosse team he helped found continues to bring NYPD officers together.

title: Colorado's Mesa Verde will return more than 4,000 sacred objects and remains of 85 Indigenous people
content:
Mesa Verde National Park is preparing to return more than 4,000 sacred objects and the remains of 85 Indigenous people in a major repatriation effort tied to Tribal history in the Southwest.
Here's what to know
In its largest repatriation effort in history, UNESCO site Mesa Verde National Park is taking a long-overdue step in returning 4,304 culturally significant objects along with the remains of 85 individuals to their rightful Tribes in Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, according to local officials, via The Denver Post.
In 1990, the federal Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) required federal agencies and institutions, like museums and universities, that receive federal funds to return Native American human remains and other cultural items to Tribal nations.
However, many of the country's most prestigious museums and universities still hold onto Indigenous objects and remains.
After conducting an inventory, Mesa Verde National Park identified ceramic bowls and jars, sandals, matting, ropes made of human hair, animal bones, feather boxes, crystals, turquoise, and buckskin bags. Tribe members can now submit repatriation requests now that the inventory is complete.
For descendant communities, repatriation is far more than a symbolic paperwork exercise. It can mean regaining stewardship of ancestors, burial items, and ceremonial objects removed from their original context—more often than not, without consent.
That makes the decision especially significant at well-known Native archaeological sites that have become tourist destinations, because it shows these areas are still part of a living cultural story for Native communities.
Tribal nations have long been trying to recover the remains of their ancestors and their sacred belongings from federal agencies, universities, and museums that acquired and kept them during eras when Native communities were shut out of the process. For these communities, the returns can support cultural preservation, spiritual practice, and healing from historical trauma.
What's being done?
Federal officials and Tribal representatives are moving through the legal and cultural steps needed to identify items, determine affiliation, and arrange their return. That work is often slow, but it is essential to getting repatriation right.
Support for cultural and environmental stewardship often goes hand in hand. If you want to back efforts that protect communities and the places they care for, it may be worth learning more about donating money to climate causes, especially those that center frontline and Indigenous leadership.
While the harm of the past and how these items fell into the wrong hands to begin with cannot be undone, returning ancestors and sacred belongings marks an important shift that recognizes respect and accountability.
"It feels amazing to know that these ancestors and different objects are going to go home and be buried, that they get to finish their journey finally," said David Hyde, Western Colorado's museum volunteer curator and collections manager. "There's no reason for Native American ancestral remains to be in museums, cabinets, or campuses. This is a long time coming."
Where can I learn more?
The articles below cover Indigenous stewardship, land, and the long legacy of displacement. They aren't specifically about repatriation, but they do show how Tribal leadership and conservation efforts across the country are rebuilding ties.
• In Arizona, the Cocopah Tribe is sparking a revival of once-pristine land with native plants.
• Across Indigenous homelands, leaders are bringing iconic native animals back to strengthen culture and grasslands.
